speechtext:
["Mr. Speaker, last week the right hon. the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker) inquired whether the government was considering something in the nature of a memorial to the children of Aberfan, Wales, and indeed to all the people in Britain to indicate the profound sympathy Canadians have felt following the heart-rending tragedy in which the village lost nearly an entire generation of children.
Information now received indicates that steps are being taken by the British authorities to rebuild the destroyed school and to provide for other rehabilitation. A public fund is being raised in Britain, and it has already reached proportions which will ensure that the future educational needs of the children of Aberfan are cared for. There would thus appear to be a limited requirement for direct assistance of this kind. The disaster's tragic effects have been in human terms.
While recognizing that nothing can compensate for the deep personal loss suffered by the families of Aberfan, the government has sought some means of expressing Canadian sympathy which would be a fitting gesture in memory of the children. In this connection we have felt also that it would be most appropriate if such a gesture also honoured
the memory of the 19 Canadian children whose lives were lost in the terrible accident at Dorion, Quebec, last month, on October 7.
The government, therefore, has decided to make a gift of $100,000 to the United Nations Children's Fund, in memory both of the children of Aberfan and of the children who died at Dorion. UNICEF will, I am confident, use this money to bring hope and health to children living in the underdeveloped countries of the world. I am sure this will be recognized and appreciated by the parents of Aberfan and Dorion alike as a most appropriate way in which we, as Canadians, can express our sympathy for the tragic loss of these children."]

Mr. Speaker, last week the right hon. the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker) inquired whether the government was considering something in the nature of a memorial to the children of Aberfan, Wales, and indeed to all the people in Britain to indicate the profound sympathy Canadians have felt following the heart-rending tragedy in which the village lost nearly an entire generation of children.
Information now received indicates that steps are being taken by the British authorities to rebuild the destroyed school and to provide for other rehabilitation. A public fund is being raised in Britain, and it has already reached proportions which will ensure that the future educational needs of the children of Aberfan are cared for. There would thus appear to be a limited requirement for direct assistance of this kind. The disaster's tragic effects have been in human terms.
While recognizing that nothing can compensate for the deep personal loss suffered by the families of Aberfan, the government has sought some means of expressing Canadian sympathy which would be a fitting gesture in memory of the children. In this connection we have felt also that it would be most appropriate if such a gesture also honoured
the memory of the 19 Canadian children whose lives were lost in the terrible accident at Dorion, Quebec, last month, on October 7.
The government, therefore, has decided to make a gift of $100,000 to the United Nations Children's Fund, in memory both of the children of Aberfan and of the children who died at Dorion. UNICEF will, I am confident, use this money to bring hope and health to children living in the underdeveloped countries of the world. Mr. Speaker, last Wednesday I asked the Minister of Labour a supplementary question

as to whether it would be mandatory upon automobile manufacturing companies to contribute to the maintenance of employees who are displaced as a result of the Canada-U.S. auto agreement. In reply the minister said "Yes, but to S.U.B. only."
In view of the fact that S.U.B. payments are established under a collective bargaining agreement and the companies pay into the fund in lieu of wages to the employees, does the minister's statement mean that the companies will contribute nothing to the transitional assistance benefit fund and that the entire burden will be borne by the treasury of Canada?

When the house rose at ten o'clock last night, Mr. Chairman, I had begun making a few observations on the state of our northern affairs. I said at that time that the north, our north, is populated by very few people, and that, in fact, the population of our north is equal only to the crowds attending a couple of football games in Vancouver.
We have a number of administrative bases around this big area scattered from Frobisher Bay in the Arctic to Inuvik in the Mackenzie area of the west. The point I put forward and
November 4, 1966

still would like to mention is that in my opinion the principle of integration and unification can very well be applied to northern services. It is true to say that we have a large number of governmental departments operating in these small communities. In the main they are doing good work, but I believe they could operate more effectively, and for the least cost, if the services were pooled or integrated.
A good deal has been said on the subject of northern education. A good deal has been done, and progress has been made. It is encouraging to note that while nine years ago only 10 per cent of native children were being educated to our standards that figure today is 85 per cent.
Although this progress is encouraging, a great deal remains to be done in coping with the basic problems that exist. One of the things that struck members of the northern affairs committee who toured the north was that the children were being educated more or less in our pattern while their parents, until quite recently, had been living in tents and igloos. Today the parents are just beginning to learn to live in houses, and I believe the committee members who went there will not disagree with me when I say that a great deal more adult education is required.
Again on this subject, we should bear in mind that it is quite difficult to educate native children in the type of schools we have in the north. In those schools they learn about things they have never seen. They read about cows and chickens, for instance, but have never seen them. In this connection I have started a modest project which is to begin shortly in my area, namely a sister school. The children attending it will exchange letters and pictures with children in a northern school. In this way the northern children can learn more about the south, and the southern children can learn more about their brothers and sisters in the north.
Housing is a grave problem in many of the remote areas. The housing which is being constructed and made available to the natives is good and, I think, practical, but we are seriously behind in what we should be attempting to undertake. Housing in these areas ranges from very good to utterly disgraceful. In some places we visited it was almost incredible how people could survive living in hovels, and I strongly urge that we speed up our efforts in providing more decent, practical housing.
Interim Supply
Something else which could be done in the north comes under the heading of the federal physical fitness program, the objective of which is to encourage athletics and participation in sports. In places like Hay River we found that this program would be very beneficial in bringing the native children together in competition and co-operation with the children of the civil servants living there. We were told by the mayor of Hay River that many of the native children tend to keep to themselves, feeling that the white children have advantages over them. He also said that when a marina had been constructed in Hay River juvenile delinquency dropped remarkably. I urge that funds be made available under the physical fitness program to encourage sports participation between all groups of children in the north.
The high cost of shipping freight to the north is a grim fact of life for people living in the northern outposts. It is true that the various departments of government make different allowances with respect to rations of imported foods provided for their staffs, but because of these differences in ration allocations that fact alone irritates the various staffs.
The cost of freight shipments is really fantastic in relation to the cost of the products being transported. For example, a dozen eggs in some areas retails at $1.25. Let us say that an egg costs 10 cents. Of that 10 cents it is calculated that 4 cents represents the cost of the egg, and almost 6 cents represents the freight cost.
The idea I have, and which I think is shared by many members of the committee, is that, just as in earlier days we had equalization of freight rates in Canada, to provide the same degree of benefit to all Canadians east and west, we should now do something like that between the north and south in order to enable the people who live and serve in the north to do so under better circumstances.
In conclusion I would like to refer briefly to the Carrothers commission report. It contains both good and dubious ingredients. One of the good recommendations is that the deputy commissioner at some future date be appointed from the elected council. Another is that a ministry of public affairs be established for the north. This, in conjunction with an educational crash program, could provide great potential for good.

November 4, 1966
Interim Supply
The decision not to divide the Arctic in two for administrative purposes is sensible. On the other hand I doubt that the recommended ten year testing period is practical. I think it is too long; five years would be adequate.
One point in the commission's recommendations of which I am highly critical is that which recommends that the top administrator be provided with additional powers and funds. Under some circumstances this would virtually make him a dictator. I believe the administrator should be elected by the people, or at least his appointment should be approved by the citizens of the north in a referendum.
The commission's report is vaguely critical of the department for its treatment of the Indian and Eskimo peoples, but it contains little mention of their land claims and treaties which are so important to them. The appointment of the executive may be necessary, but there should be council control over the executive. I think hon. members would be greatly interested to get the reactions of the people in the north to the commission's recommendations.
[DOT] (11:50 a.m.)
In the main I think the report is good, but it has these drawbacks I have mentioned. Finally, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say that we have very great problems in the north, no matter who is administering the area. Basically the problems come down to those of time and space. Modem science and modern transportation is beginning to bridge the problem of space; and education, together with useful employment, is beginning to meet the problem of time

that is, the difference between the old native outlook and the advent of our form of civilization. I think something good is being done in the north. I commend the minister as a very active minister in that regard. A great deal, however, remains to be tackled. Far from easing up in our efforts there, I think we should press forward with them.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to participate in the debate at this time I did not know I would have the privilege of using a new term in respect of this process that is going through the mind of the Minister of National Defence, and that what we should now talk about is amalgamation. I do not know whether this is an attempt to clarify the confusion which exists not only in his mind but also in the minds of all the servicemen and the public of Canada, concerning what he means or what he intends to do with

regard to the defence forces of Canada. What does he intend to do? Does he intend to put them into Kelly green outfits, with some sort of a hat? Or, how does he intend to torpedo or scupper them in so far as their effectiveness is concerned?
One of my very great friends, a former serviceman, said to me one day, "Yes, it is conceivable that Canada might have the highest paid mercenaries in the world, with all the loyalty and affection there is for the service of mercenaries". This is a serious reflection upon the state of the morale of Canada's defence forces, and is something which I feel the minister knows nothing about. This has to do with the morale that is required of fighting men who have gone through the experience of war. This is something which is being denied by those-and I do not question their motives at all-who feel that morale and a certain esprit de corps in a military unit is meaningless.
The millions, or hundreds of thousands of men in this country, who in the main are protesting against this, have gone through that experience. What is that additional something that is in a man's mind when, in the crunch, he has a particular incentive along with his colleagues and his unit-a pride in his uniform and a pride in the service? Those of us who consider these motives today are airily dismissed as being out of date by people who know nothing about it and who have not experienced it. All it would require is for them to have gone through some of the same experiences.
I am not talking about the integration of the command structure of the forces; that is a separate subject. A great deal has been said about this, and as far back as 1958 I have been saying that this would have to be done in certain sectors. That being so, however, I do not feel we should go at a gallop merely for the sake of unification and integration. Today we have had the warning from the required to mobilize, materiel command there were a crunch or crisis and we were required to mobilize, Materiel Command could not meet the strain. There have been men who have far more experience than the minister has had in military affairs, who understand the administration of armies, who understand the administration of armed forces or field formations and who understand all the difficulties, and these men in great earnestness say to the minister we should now pause to examine what we have done: Let us test it.
November 4, 1966

Interim Supply
There is a good deal oi good in what may have been done in so far as integration is concerned, but surely to goodness there is nothing to cause the minister to carry on at a mad gallop and refuse the advice of professional soldiers, airmen and sailors who have gone to the top of the service, not merely because of their years of service, not because of an old school tie, but because of their record of performance. The majority of these men were tested in the fire of battle and in the stress and strain of war, something the minister knows nothing about. This is the difficulty I find. I say that if these men tell the minister we must now pause and examine what we have done, that we must test it in exercises and that we must find the weaknesses, then he is nothing but foolhardy when he disregards this advice.
When we build a building do we test the foundation after we have put the roof on, after we have put the windows in, and after we have everything painted and ready for occupancy? That is precisely what the minister wants to do with regard to the Canadian armed forces. As my colleague the hon. member for Kamloops so ably pointed out last night in one of the best speeches on this subject, this matter gives us the greatest concern. Those men who were in command positions when the white paper came out-a document which apparently said a great deal more to the author than it did to the public-are gone, all gone. Why? Because they would not go down the straight and narrow confines of some undefined something which has been kept locked in the minister's breast, in so far as integration and unification are concerned.
The minister can dismiss this with an airy smile, if he wants to, but I should like to tell him of something which happened last week-and this has been repeated to me by many people. A corporal with many years service in the army came in for re-engagement and he saw his commanding officer. Incidentally, the commanding officer told me he was one of the best N.C.O.s he had. The corporal said "I have been serving in the Canadian army and I desire to re-engage in the Canadian army. If I re-engage am I re-engaging in the Canadian army or what am I re-engaging in?" The commanding officer said to him, "I am sorry, but I cannot tell you to what force you would belong if you re-engaged". He did not re-engage.
[DOT] (12 noon)
Oh, oh.

The hon. member for
Chicoutimi can laugh, but the information I have was given to me by a gentleman who has a great deal more experience than that hon. member.
Give us an example.

There are many examples I could give in respect, not only of N.C.O.s but of officers at the junior and middle levels. This type of thing is happening throughout the services at all levels, and anyone who denies that fact is either deliberately misrepresenting the situation or is completely ignorant.
What is the percentage of this occurrence?

Whenever we refer to reengagement or re-enlistment the statistics can be confusing. We know these re-enlistments have been declining. The number of personnel in our forces has been declining month after month and the minister and those speaking on his behalf know they are wrong when they say our rate of recruitment is satisfactory. Could a recruit possibly replace efficiently a veteran of 12 or 15 years experience, whether he is an N.C.O. or an officer? The obvious answer is that he could not. Are we going to put recruits on our destroyers as technicians immediately after their enlistment? We know we are short of technicians because the minister finally admitted that more and more ships are being tied up because of the lack of trained personnel. That fact was denied for a long period of time. The members in this house were treated as carping fools by the minister and those who speak on his behalf, because we dared to point out these things.
Oh, oh.

The hon. member for
Chicoutimi may laugh but I invite him to take a meaningful trip and visit these servicemen to find out what the situation actually is.
Mr. Chairman- [English]

The hon. member should take his seat because I have the floor. He can

make his speech when I am finished because there will be plenty of time during this debate. He has not occupied enough of the time of this house as yet.
I hope you will hear my speech.
I invite the hon. member to make some contribution to this debate.
That would be sheer nonsense.
You will see.

Let me tell the hon. member that if we continue in this fashion so far as national defence is concerned, it will take us at least half a generation to replace the trained men in order to maintain the standard of efficiency as it was 18 months ago.
Let me say this to the minister who criticized the speech of my colleague, the hon. member for Kamloops-
Mr. Chairman-
The hon. member has the right to his own opinion, but let me assure him that I base mine on experience, knowledge and communication.
The next thing will be conscription.

The minister has suggested that we should only debate unification. I suggest the minister has not one iota of an idea as to what he means by unification. This is a complete mystery, in spite of the fact there have been leaks and puffy articles by some of the establishment writers. Strangely enough, there have been some senior officers travelling around the country singing hosannas about the policy of unification, but none of them would dare criticize this policy because to do so would be to place themselves in peril. None of the senior officers criticized the unification policy publicly before retiring or being fired. Let me contradict the statement that has been made to the effect that Admiral Landymore was fired because he publicly criticized the minister. The minister is well aware of the chronology of these events. He knows that Rear Admiral Landymore was relieved of his duties or asked to resign prior to any public statement he made. The minister is well aware of this fact.
That is correct.

I am glad to hear the minister say that, because perhaps now the press will correct the misconception it created. Any statement to the effect that Rear Admiral Landymore was fired after he criticized defence policy publicly is downright misrepresentation, because that did not happen. It is strange how the minister and his sycophants have been prepared to leave that impression. The minister has had other senior officers of the forces fired before they had even opened their mouths, including Admiral Dyer, General Fleury and General Moncel, yet he has the gall to say that these officers retired as the result of a mutual understanding.
That is correct.
I should like to know who was the author of that gobbledygook, the minister or those who write on his behalf. I should like to hear explanations regarding some other retirements.
You are not going to.

I have heard different versions as to what took place. It is indeed strange that only one man should be right and all the rest wrong. Many senior officers have retired who have not spoken up, but most of them will tell you privately that they retired ahead of time and were glad to do so. Some of these men possess more military knowledge and experience in the administration of military affairs in their little finger than the minister will ever possess, and that goes for most of his personal advisers as well. These men were dismissed out of hand because they dared to say that we should examine the situation to see whether or not the proposed path was the right one.
The cost of Canada's defence forces represents almost 25 per cent of our national budget. This is important from a purely financial point of view; yet they are prepared to deal in a cavalier manner with the whole structure and essence of these forces.
We are told today that we are discussing the details of unification or, as it is now termed, amalgamation, but we are not to receive any explanation until after we have accepted this measure in principle. Surely that is a mockery of parliamentary procedure. This is an attitude that can only be described as-I was going to call it intellectual arrogance, but I will not compliment it by that description. I invite the minister to
November 4, 1966

appear before the defence committee to explain his stand. Let us discuss this measure in a meaningful way with those people who are in agreement and those who are in opposition, so that we can truly assess it. Let us do that rather than accept it in principle in this house. The minister wants to play cards, but he wants to use a stacked deck. That is how sure he is of his position.
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
I challenge the minister to appear before the defence committee prior to our discussing this matter in the house. Then we could question him about unification and some of the things that have been done since mid-June this year. We should like to know the opinions put forward by men who counselled the minister three years before integration, in order that our study of this question may be complete. The minister received their advice-some of these witnesses gave this evidence to the defence committee-and then they were relieved of their duties. We want an explanation of this.
With regard to the defence committee reconvening and dealing with this question, the minister knows full well the shenanigans that went on at the time the committee was completing its consideration of the departmental estimates. There was a recommendation from the steering committee, composed of the chairman of the committee, the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.), the hon. member for Welland, the hon. member for Lambton West and the hon. member for Renfrew North, that the committee go into in-camera sessions to consider the evidence that had been presented to it in order to make a report.
This matter was under consideration. The chairman had brought forward that item of business, but he was prepared to accept a motion by a member who had rarely attended the meetings of the defence committee that the estimates should be reported back to the house forthwith without comment. I shall not deal with all the protests raised at that time. But I say that this was an inspired move, a coldly calculated move that brings no credit to the government members of the committee, its chairman or the government members of the steering committee, because they were prepared at that time to swallow their convictions and proceed against their own recommendation.
I want to know whether at that time the chairman of the committee had been informed directly or indirectly that Admiral
Interim Supply
Landymore's brief had been seriously amended. I have copies of the two versions of the brief tabled by the minister. As the one who was doing most of the questioning on the matter of morale in the forces, I can say definitely that the innocuous evidence the admiral was permitted to give in his brief with regard to the morale of the men under his command misled, and was designed to mislead, the committee. The minister must accept full responsibility for this; it was his responsibility all the way through. It was done, at the minister's behest, by someone else: He knew about it.
I say that if the chairman of the committee knew of this prior to the final consideration of the estimates, he was duty bound to tell the other members of the steering committee that he had received information that this complaint had been made. It is up to the hon. member for Victoria, B.C., to advise this house just where he stood in this regard and when he had knowledge of the amending of Admiral Landymore's brief. If that hon. member did know about it, I say it was his duty as chairman of the committee, which is responsible not to the minister, not to the government but to this house, to acquaint the committee of those facts. Knowledge of the facts could materially have affected the way the committee proceeded thereafter. I hope the hon. member will tell us in due course precisely when he knew that this brief had been amended.
The other night the hon. member for Leeds, as reported at page 9413 of Hansard, came forth with a most fantastic interpretation of the relationship of ministers to committees, and the status of committees. I suppose the hon. member believes that a committee should be just a little blueprint organization for ministerial ukases and ministerial views. This is what the hon. member for Leeds said:
I think the Minister of National Defence and his department have the responsibility to determine how soon the committee meets.
The minister and his departmental officials shall determine when a house committee shall meet?-what arrant nonsense. I would suggest that the hon. member for Leeds take another look at his position as a member of his house. If he wants to be one of a herd of docile cattle, let him be that; but I suggest that this is not the role of hon. members whether in the house or in committee. It is always interesting to see the transformation in attitude when an hon. member who was in

November 4, 1966

opposition finds himself on the government side of the house. I should like to ask the hon. member for Leeds whether when he was in opposition he subscribed to the theory that he expounded the other night with regard to when a committee should meet, and whether it should be at the behest of a minister and his officials.
I have spoken about the results of the minister's lack of communication as to what he means precisely by unification and integration. The morale of the forces is down; there are no two ways about this. This is the most regrettable thing I can possibly say, because I have great admiration for our defence forces and an ardent desire to see that they are the best possible, that they are men who will be proud to represent Canada and proud of their service and uniform.
The navy has been torpedoed; there is no doubt about that. The minister can shake his head, but I know some of the details of the minister's visit to Halifax and I know something about the reception he received. He has not convinced the navy that it has not been torpedoed, neither the ratings nor officers. The only reason the minister received subdued opposition was because of the sense of discipline and honour of the men concerned; otherwise his reception would have been much different.
They would have tarred and feathered him and thrown him out.

We are in a similar position in so far as the air force is concerned, although the situation in that service has not accelerated to the same degree as in the navy.
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)
The minister does not know how he will man his CF-5's when and if they come into service, and that question has to be reviewed also. He does not know whether he can put in an airlift on the Hercules, when the R.C.A.F. gets its full complement, and whether he will find sufficient crews to man the aircraft. If the debilitating retirement from the air force continues, he will not have the crews and the back-up crews for transport command. This is the result of some of the nonsensical policies that have been carried out. The minister can grin, but if he could get rid for a moment of that sort of self-induced aura of righteousness, I would remind him of the days when he was sitting opposite as the defence critic, and the days of the famous disclosed plan. It was then as senseless as it

is now; the only trouble is that now we are unfortunately seeing some of those plans being put into action, or at least attempted.
I will say to the minister in all sincerity that I think his performance in this regard has been regrettable. I will be temperate in my language and only say that the minister's actions have in some cases been contemptible. Not only have they been contemptible to this house, but also contemptuous of this house. They have been contemptuous of the services and of the men that he leads as the Minister of National Defence. I would hate to be in his shoes and ultimately to have to account for the comments of the men who have retired. These are men on whose abilities our services of the future will have to rely. They have gone because they do not wish to have anything more to do with it. And what of the men whose sons are growing up with their fathers' military tradition? There are many such fathers, men who have just retired or are about to retire who have said to me: "I am advising my son not to enter the services."

Mr. Chairman, I will just complete my sentence. If there is anything that reflects more vividly the present state of morality in the forces it is the father who has a proud record in the services telling his son, "The services are not for you".
Will the hon. member permit me to ask him a question?
Mr. Chairman, my time is up, but if the committee will allow me more time I will answer the hon. member's question.

Mr. Chairman, I arrived while the hon. member was on his feet and I did not hear his entire speech. However, I came in at a moment when he was referring to me. He asked when I was going to stand up and give an explanation concerning certain information which had been given to me by Admiral Landymore. I wonder whether the hon. member, who is the vice chairman of the defence committee and who was not in the house last night when I was speaking-
I was.

I do not think you were in your seat when I was speaking. I was asked the
November 4, 1966

same question by another hon. member. I wonder if the hon. member for Edmonton West has read my answer which appears at page 9521 of Hansard. There is nothing further I can add to what appears there.

Mr. Chairman, may I just give a brief answer. First of all, I was in the house during the whole time of the hon. member's speech. However, my questions were much more precise than the question put to the hon. member previously. I asked him whether he had any direct or indirect information on the modifications in Admiral Landymore's speech, and at what time did this occur prior to the last meeting of the defence committee?
Answer.

November 4, 1966
Interim Supply
in an attempt to influence the administration of the nation. Militarism should not be carried too far in our country. The minister made alterations, changes in the reports of Admiral Landymore, Admiral Brock or someone else; I think that was much more his responsibility since he assumes, with his colleagues of the cabinet, the responsibility for the defence of our country, and his responsibility is certainly more normal than that of an admiral who has not been elected to administer but appointed to look after the defence of our country.
The opposition complains, Mr. Chairman, that it did not have the opportunity to discuss these things, that it was not well informed. Well, I went to the source and I was shocked to find that there had been thousands of press releases, of witnesses summoned, that there had been at least a hundred meetings of that committee dealing with defence and that hundreds of witnesses had been summoned, in short that there had been hundreds of advisors around the minister to help him form an opinion and prepare his white paper. What more do we want? Let the government assume its responsibilities; if it meets with failure, it will be responsible to the Canadian people. But I believe it must assume its responsibilities, courageously, and not be impressed by those who have divergent views.
I do not say that everything suggested by the opposition is worthless, Mr. Chairman. There are worthy suggestions and I also think that the minister will be willing to hear them and take them into consideration in due time.
A few days ago, someone raised in the house an incident, which created a greater stir than it should have probably, concerning a newspaper report saying that this was, in fact, a kind of underhanded war against the change in long-standing habits, that some people wanted to retain, especially for the navy, its British protestant control. I found that fantastic and unthinkable at the time but the more I listen to the debate, the more I wonder whether another underhanded war is not being waged against those who were recently appointed to take charge of our Canadian army, who displayed discipline, who therefore accept integration and unification prescribed by the government, as every good soldier should do, in my opinion.
I wonder if all the criticism or filibuster that is going on would not be aimed precisely at waging a sneaky war on those people who see their duty and know that it is not up to

them to dictate government policy on defence matters.
Mr. Chairman, I believe there is an underlying preoccupation, that I might call instinctive, on the part of members of the opposition, which simply consists in bringing about the eventual downfall of the hon. minister and the government. It is only natural for the opposition to try and destroy a member of the cabinet, but the morale of the armed forces should not be sacrificed for this purpose; one should not resort to prompting the people responsible for our country's defence to rebellion in order to achieve this objective; it should not be achieved by undermining the sense of discipline which those who are responsible for our country's defence, under government orders, must have.
Mr. Chairman, it is my opinion that the official opposition is to be blamed for having sowed the seeds of insubordination among servicemen during this debate.
Not at all.
I say it again, although this does not please the hon. member for Edmonton West, the hon. minister must assume his responsibilities-
We also have responsibilities.

-and he must assume them with his colleagues in the cabinet.
I feel that these incidents will very shortly prove to be unfortunate for national defence services. I repeat once again that if the hon. minister is wrong, the Canadian people will call him to account.
Mr. Chairman, I submit that it is high time to quell this admirals' reform. I am one of those who support the firmness shown by the hon. Minister of National Defence, even though no one in the house can foresee the results of unification and integration. We are faced with a problem, but we must take everything into consideration: some things are sure, others are not. Once again, this is a situation where the hon. minister must accept his responsibilities, and I am one of those who mean to give him every possible opportunity to assume them. If he errs, we will call upon him to account for his action; that will be our role in due time. Mr. Chairman, that is all I had to say with respect to integration and unification of the armed forces.
I would now like to call the attention of the house to a problem which will undoubtedly have a local connotation, but it is of
November 4, 1966

such scope that it can have at least provincial, if not national, repercussions. Therefore, I want to raise it in the house.
The Department of Transport last year, undertook dredging operations in the St. Lawrence channel, not too far from my constituency, in what is called lake St. Peter. Thousands of tons of clay were dredged from the bottom of the channel, which is quite normal. But what is not normal is that the stuff was dumped along the shore creating a sort of isthmus or Sahara desert in lake St. Peter which resulted in extensive damage to nearby properties. This spoiled the landscape to the point where it now offers a view which is absolutely hideous. In view of the fact that this is along a main highway, the Montreal-Quebec highway, it is an extremely unpleasant surprise for tourists going through there.
Mr. Chairman, I mention this because it seems that virtually all means to correct the situation have been exhausted. As early as May or June last, I made representations to the Departments of Transport and Public Works on behalf of the owners of water lots who invested considerable amounts of money in them.
[DOT] (12:40 p.m.)
I have a list of the owners of water lots. This is a place where people spend the summer. Houses have been built there, some valued at over $100,000; others are less expensive, but all the property in this one little spot is worth at least half a million dollars. The access to the beach, the view and the scenery have been spoilt by a dump of refuse from the river and the lake. This is a very ugly sight for all who go that way.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a protest to the government. I have already asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pick-ersgill) and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mcllraith) to remedy the situation. I should like to say that I am dissatisfied with the answer I have received. I am told that the contractor is the one who made a mistake and that he is ready to spend $4,000 to $5,000 to correct it. The contractor certainly must have done this work under the direction of government engineers. It is incredible that there should be in this department such stupid engineers, who understand so little the importance of our beautiful scenery that they would allow it to be spoiled in this way.
I have before me a request signed by all the owners of water lots. I have the claims 23033-604
Interim Supply
and the figures. They had the damage assessed and up until now these claims have been flatly rejected. It seems that everyone wants to wash his hands of it. The Department of Public Works says that the one to blame is the McNamara Company Quebec Limited who did the work for the St. Lawrence ship channel division of the Department of Transport. And the McNamara company says: The fault lies with the engineers who gave us instructions; we obeyed them.
Mr. Chairman, I want to protest against that and warn the minister that we shall not stand such conditions any longer. We are going to take all legal steps available to us so as to obtain a review of the situation, unless the minister decides to do justice to the owners of water lots.
I am sure that if the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Public Works were to visit that landscape, one of the most beautiful in the province of Quebec, and see the shameless and unimaginable way it has been marred, they would be shocked and would see that the necessary steps be immediately taken in order to remedy the situation at once.
I urge the government, before the water lot owners succeed in stirring up public opinion more seriously than they are doing now, to take the necessary steps so as to take care of this situation and so that those properties at least, which in some cases have been built at enormous cost and privation, be not depreciated for ever.
Mr. Chairman, those are the two things I wished to point out. With all possible discretion, I urge all those having suggestions to make in regard to unification, integration, to always consider, while making them, their actual possible effects upon the morale of this country's forces, upon the sense of discipline they should have and not to forget that this is a concern that should transcend partisan considerations.

Opening with the remarks I had intended starting with, I hope that the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.), who is behind the curtain, will listen, because I want to start by referring to the speech he made last night. I asked my colleagues in the house last night to let me know when the hon. member spoke, but unfortunately I was before a committee and could not leave. It was, of course, with eager anticipation that I read the hon. member's speech in Hansard

November 4, 1966
Interim Supply
this morning. I was disappointed and, as a matter of fact, disgusted to read that he, the chairman of the defence committee, had nothing to say.
The hon. member made three points. The first one supported the stand of the Minister of National Defence to the effect that officers and officials of departments giving evidence before the defence committee may give only that evidence which the minister will allow them to give. I have been to hundreds of committee meetings where officials have appeared and given evidence freely. At any point where it appeared that a question from a member of the committee touched on a policy matter the chairman of the committee would intervene, or the official giving the evidence would simply say that the question referred to a matter of policy which he did not feel he should comment on. If the chairman of the defence committee is of the view that officials of the department may not give evidence even of facts, what is the value of calling such people before the committee? Are they to say exactly what the minister wants them to say about facts, or an interpretation of the facts? At any rate, this whole subject was the first point brought up by the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.).
Next he was accusing Admiral Brock of playing politics. Mr. Chairman, people such as Admiral Brock and others who have recently retired have a duty, when asked by members of parliament from any party for advice, to give it. I say that giving advice when asked for it is to the credit of Admiral Brock. It is to the credit of the Conservative party that is has sought advice from knowledgeable people. Was General Foulkes who sought the Liberal nomination in Victoria two years ago playing politics by virtue of writing certain articles?
A few minutes ago when the hon. member for Edmonton West gave the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.), the chairman of the defence committee, a clear opportunity to answer certain questions, he stood up but made no effort to answer those questions. The hon. member for Edmonton West had asked whether the chairman of the defence committee had any knowledge, directly or indirectly, of the fact that Admiral Landymore's testimony had been tampered with, or of the fact that any other officers' evidence had been tampered with. It was the duty of the chairman of the committee at least to bring this matter to the attention of the steering committee. He had a duty and a right, under certain circumstances, to call the defence committee into

being again and explain to it the knowledge he has. Surely every member of the defence committee ought to know to what extent he has been misled, or to what extent pertinent information has been withheld from him.
I think it was the duty also of the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) to let his constituents know where he stands on the question of unification. To my knowledge, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) has made no public statement as to his position in this whole matter. Surely as an elected member he has a dual duty to let the opposition and the defence committee know his position in this matter. There have been many invitations to the hon. member to make his position known, but so far he has declined to do so.
Also, I should be interested to know the kinds of answers he gives to people writing to him. For instance, the letter I got from the air force officers association asks certain questions. A copy of the letter was sent to the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.).
Having referred to the speech of the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) 1 cannot refrain from commenting on another speech made from the other side of the house by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra. At the risk of mentioning that speech, and therefore upgrading it to the point where it is worthy of mention, I want to say that in my opinion that speech is the embodiment of inanity. What is wrong with the Conservative party's preparing a policy statement on defence, or preparing papers on plausible party positions relating to defence? What is wrong with consulting knowledgeable people to prepare our policy position? The position taken by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra contained the inference that there was some deep, dark, secret plot. In my opinion he did nothing but waste the time of the house.
As a contrast I found the speech by the Associate Minister of National Defence very interesting reading. I do not agree with what he said, but he had good, debatable points, and I commend him for the moderate manner in which he gave his views. What a difference there would be in our position with regard to defence today if the associate minister were the minister of national defence. I want to take issue, however, with one point he raised when, at page 9395 of Hansard he referred to an article written by General Foulkes which appeared in the Star Weekly Magazine of October 14,	1961, and wherein General
Foulkes says:
We need one single armed service under one supreme chief of staff in one uniform.
November 4, 1966

As the Associate Minister of National Defence has said, it is proper for him and for anybody else to seek advice from knowledgeable people, therefore it was proper for him to take advice from a person as knowledgeable as General Foulkes.
I suggest to the Associate Minister of National Defence, however, that he bring himself up to date. I refer to an article in the Ottawa Journal of Thursday, October 13, 1966 by the same General Charles Foulkes, from which I shall quote a few excerpts. First:
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
One of the aspects of integration, which is relatively unimportant but which is causing some resentment in the services is the announced intention to force the servicemen into a neutral uniform by 1967. Perhaps this is to be part of the "centennial" celebrations to show that Canada still maintains, what a pundit once referred to, as "the best dressed, best fed, best paid, but poorest equipped force in the west."
Again 1 quote from this article by General Foulkes:
Since any acceptable integration scheme calls for the continuation of regiments of soldiers, squadrons of aircraft and flotillas of ships, the servicemen in these combat formations must continue to wear the appropriate combat uniform.
Again quoting from this article:
We should not be mesmerized by the idea that a common uniform will ensure a happy, contented and efficient integrated service.
Quoting still further from the article:
The minister has not been forthright in informing the services and the public of the true and real extent of the integration plot.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I hope that the Associate Minister of National Defence being a fair minded person, as I know he is, will take some advice from the same person from whom he apparently took advice in 1961.
I contend that the Minister of National Defence has been operating by propaganda and press releases issued by some of the officials in his department. I maintain he has deliberately tried to confuse the people of Canada as to integration and as to unification. Even in the bill which he introduced today he avoided using the word "unification", and coined a new one, "amalgamation".
Now, Mr. Chairman, I would like to read a long editorial which appeared in the Daily Colonist on Sunday, October 2, and which I could not put better in my own words. It is headed, "Fiction and Fact" and reads:
One of the first things Mr. Paul Hellyer did when he became Minister of National Defence in April, 1963, was to establish what can only be described 23033-6041
Interim Supply
as a personal propaganda section in his office under former R.C.A.F. Group Captain William Lee.
Since that time Mr. Lee has been a very busy fellow indeed. Operating under the title of special assistant to the Minister of National Defence he has sent out what now must amount to tons of photostats, clippings or copies of every editorial, article or news commentary appearing in Canada or elsewhere which made favourable mention of his minister.
He got a new Xerox machine.

I think he would need more than one Xerox. The editorial continues:
These items, enclosed in O.H.M.S. envelopes and franked by the minister, have been pouring out of national defence headquarters into newspaper, radio and television offices throughout the country in an ever-increasing stream.
If it is to be assumed that this is not propaganda but simply information which is being dispensed by Mr. Lee then it must be assumed that if the material goes out under the Minister of National Defence's initial on the envelope the contents are factually accurate.
The validity of this assumption, however, can be quite easily challenged by a cursory glance at some of the articles which have gone out with the minister's official blessing.
As but one example: At the end of 1964 or early 1965 Mr. Hellyer's propaganda machine sent out a lengthy news commentary by the Ottawa correspondent of one of the international news services. The article was highly complimentary to Mr. Hellyer and made a number of assertions well calculated to appease any doubts the public may have held regarding the defence policy followed by the present government.
Apart from completely confusing the integration-unification issue the author makes the following points on which some editorial comment is justified.
Point: The new commander in chief of the armed forces has assembled a team of the best military minds available to mould the new single service force.
Comment: More than a dozen of the most senior army, navy and air force officers who were what must have been the best military minds in Canada at that time have now either been retired or fired.
Point: Mr, Hellyer presented the armed forces with a $1.5 billion Christmas (1964) present that included six new warships.
Comment: Four of these ships have not yet been ordered. In fact the orders for four ships comparable to the ones mentioned were cancelled.
Point: "Hellyer's greatest accomplishment, however, was winning the respect and admiration of the services for his radical face-lifting operation."
Comment: Mr. Hellyer's recent experience in Halifax and the fact that all three services are far, almost dangerously, under strength would seem to give the lie to this point.
May I interject for a moment, Mr. Chairman, to extend an invitation to the minister that he, perhaps accompanied by the chairman of the defence committee, visit the base

November 4, 1966
Interim Supply
at Esquimalt. However, so that the public will not again be misled or confused, I would urge him to let the press accompany him so that we can have a first-hand account of the warm reception he will receive there.
Continuing to read from the editorial:
Point: Anti-submarine warfare operations have now been directed by a central command, thus showing how effectively Mr. Hellyer's integration policy is working.
Comment: A.S.W. operations have been carried out by an integrated navy and air force command since 1958-five years before Mr. Hellyer took
office.
Point: Two countries, one a major world power, will launch their own unification plans, based on the Canadian program. In 1965 "Hellyer, clearly, has been a pacemaker for his counterparts in other nations."
I suggest that the minister should read the white paper issued in New Zealand this year, which no doubt was drafted with some knowledge of what the Minister of National Defence has done in Canada, and he will see in that white paper that unification is categorically rejected.
The last paragraph in the editorial reads:
Point: "The greatest concern among military circles today (1964) is that Hellyer may be promoted out of defence and into another cabinet portfolio too soon."
Comment on this one is surely unnecessary.
For the benefit of those who are hungry, Mr. Chairman, may I ask that we suspend our sitting for a lunch hour?

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Batten in the chair:

Mr. Chairman, before the luncheon recess I explained how the minister, through very clever propaganda, had misled and confused the people of Canada with regard to integration and unification. There
November 4, 1966

November 4, 1966
Interim Supply
which was incomplete, inadequate and perhaps misleading on the basis of the information it received. As soon as it came to the attention of the chairman that the evidence presented to the committee, on which the report to the house was based, had been altered, it was his duty to notify at least the steering committee and reconvene the committee.
I feel very strongly that the government should seriously consider allowing this matter to be fully discussed by that committee. The committee, should be permitted to call these senior officers in the armed forces, who have left for various reasons and who disagree with the minister's policy, to give their evidence.
There are many questions which should be answered before this house is asked to vote approval of the principle of unification. I have a copy of a letter dated October 26 from the Air Force Officers Association of Vancouver Island which lends support to this suggestion. Let me read an excerpt from the letter:
Constitutionally our association must refrain from engaging in activities which engender political or pressure-group overtones. Our membership, however, has expressed a very deep concern that legislation about to be introduced, dealing with the further integration and the ultimate unification of the armed forces of Canada might prove detrimental to the defence of Canada.
It is the consensus of the association that before any further steps in this direction are taken by our government, the aims and objectives of such proposed legislation be clarified and defined for the benefit of the Canadian people. Accordingly, I have been directed to submit the following questions, all of which are considered to be deserving of public answer, to you:
(1) What is the meaning of 'integration'?
(2) What is the meaning of 'unification'?
(3)	What advantages will accrue under 'unification' which are not already in being under the integrated three-service system?
(4)	How will 'unification' increase service efficiency?
(5)	To what extent will the proposed 'unified' force be effective in the defence of Canada?
(6)	To what extent and by what means will 'unification' introduce financial economies to the taxpayer?
(7)	How will 'unification' affect service morale?
(8)	To what extent is the recent loss of many experienced personnel, at all levels of the three services, attributable to 'integration' and 'unification' policies already introduced?
The last sentence of this letter is as follows:
However, since it is impossible for the Canadian public to form or voice an opinion without first having available the information covered by the above questions, our association is obliged to urge

that such legislation be withheld until the answers have been provided.
There is great concern among the Canadian people about the steps the minister is proposing because it is felt they may permanently affect the security of Canada and the position of Canada in the community of nations. I urge the minister and the government, with all sincerity, to consider the referral of this question to the defence committee before asking parliament to give approval to the principle of a bill for unification. The government should not be hesitant in any way to do this. Surely, the minister and the government must consider this one of the most important measures to come before parliament because of its possible effect on Canada's future. Why should we rush this bill through to provide unification? As the Leader of the official Opposition has said, once an egg has been scrambled you cannot unscramble it.
Surely all members on all sides of the house will support the suggestion that this matter be referred to the defence committee before we approve it in principle. With all the sincerity at my command, I urge the minister and the government to give serious consideration to this request which has come from many concerned organizations and people across this land.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to take advantage of this occasion to say a few words about a question which clearly has been of interest to this house. I refer to the automobile program and, in particular, recently discussed arrangements between the Studebaker and Volkswagen companies.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
There has been, it is quite clear, a large measure of misunderstanding in relation to the automotive program itself. I think it would be helpful if I were to set out simply and concisely some of the key facts in relation to this program, and try to answer some of the questions in rather greater detail than perhaps is possible on orders of the day. It has been asked whether the law allows a Canadian motor vehicle manufacturer to import vehicles duty free from a producer in any other country. The answer, quite simply, is yes. The authority for this under the present program is Tariff Item No. 95000, established by P.C. 1965-100 issued in the Canada Gazette and tabled in the house in February, 1965. To qualify for the right to import vehicles duty free, a Canadian vehicle manufacturer must meet certain clearly defined conditions described in Tariff Item No. 95000
November 4, 1966

and in the letter of commitment to the government.
The question then arises as to whether the legal right of a Canadian vehicle producer to import duty free from any foreign source was contemplated when the program was drawn up, or did it occur because of a loophole in the law? The answer is that the program was drawn up to provide specifically for this right. If the right to import vehicles duty free were limited to trade between companies which were affiliated by common ownership or control, or which were producing the same make of vehicle, it would have discriminated against many small Canadian manufacturers which do not have corporate manufacturing links abroad. Hon. members should know that there are more than 25 small Canadian vehicle producers right across the country which do not have corporate affiliates abroad and which produce their own makes, but which are now operating successfully under the program. Some of these independent Canadian companies have been actively exploring arrangements with vehicle producers in the United States and overseas countries which would permit them further to expand and specialize their Canadian production. I would ask whether there is any fundamental difference in terms of desirable economic results for such an arrangement between, say, General Motors and its United States parent or, on the other hand, an independent small producer in Canada and a firm in France, Italy or Germany?
Another question asked was whether Studebaker was the beneficiary of any special arrangement entered into with the government to enable that company to import a certain number of Volkswagens duty free. The answer is that no special arrangements were made to accommodate Studebaker in this respect. It was open to Studebaker, as it was to any other vehicle producer in Canada, to earn this right by meeting and fulfilling the conditions under the program. This gives rise, of course, to the question of how an arrangement such as the one we are considering, that between Studebaker and Volkswagen, helps Canada; or in other words, how does it help to meet the objectives of the automotive program? The key objectives of the automotive program are, as I think has been outlined on a number of occasions: to increase production in Canada; to increase employment in Canada; to increase exports from Canada; to make possible lower costs of production in Canada by encouraging large scale output and increased specialization, and
Interim Supply
finally, to help consumers in Canada benefit from lower costs of production which through the forces of competition in the market lead to bringing Canadian motor vehicle prices more into line with prices charged in other countries.
In order to qualify for the right to import automotive products duty free Studebaker, like any other company, had to increase its output and market its increased output at home or abroad. This Studebaker did in large volume. It expanded its production in Canada from 7,000 to 17,000 vehicles, a large proportion of which, of course, it sold abroad. In this way, it earned the right to import duty free a certain value of cars and original equipment parts. Studebaker, as I have already stated, was free to import cars and original equipment parts from any source. Some of these came from its affiliated company in the United States, and when its United States affiliate stopped producing vehicles Studebaker chose to import from Germany. Unfortunately, Studebaker did not find it possible to continue as a producer of vehicles in Canada, but for a period of two years Studebaker of Canada produced and sold more cars than ever before. The company kept 700 Canadians directly employed, and many more through its production in Canada of parts, materials and services. The automotive program, and the import rights which it made available, made it possible for Studebaker to carry on production in Canada from 1964 to 1966.
It has been suggested that the arrangements between Studebaker and Volkswagen had the result of increasing Volkswagen imports to Canada to the detriment of automotive production and employment in Canada. I would say to the committee that one can unequivocally state that this is not so. Sales of Volkswagens in Canada have been remarkably stable since the automotive program was introduced. What happened was that a limited number of Volkswagens, which would in any event have been imported to meet the taste of Canadians who like these small cars, were imported free of duty. Two points emerge from these facts: Canadian production and employment did not suffer in any way; and the automotive program is helping Canadian producers become more competitive so that they can compete more effectively even with duty free Volkswagens.
The question has also been asked: Who receives benefits from the savings in duty on automotive products imported free under the

November 4, 1966
Interim Supply
program? Savings in the payment of duties are like any other savings in production costs as far as a company is concerned. Such savings permit a company to compete more effectively in the market place, and it is such competition which protects the consumer. I have on earlier occasions given the house facts about prices to show how Canadian consumers benefited from the program in the first two model years of its operation. In the case of Studebaker, which obtained the main saving from the arrangement with Volkswagen, the prices of its automobiles were trimmed in their last year of production. In the case of Volkswagen, it is interesting to note that in the current model year they raised their United States price but held the price line in Canada. I would ask whether it is too much to conclude that, in the final analysis, it is the Canadian consumer who benefits when customs duties are brought down.
[DOT] (2:30 p.m.)
The question has also been asked whether Studebaker is still entitled to import vehicles free of duty. The answer is no. Studebaker no longer qualifies because it is not at present a producer of motor vehicles.
In conclusion, I should like to reiterate the point I made earlier in relation to the legal right and the justification for the entitlement of Canadian vehicle producers to import vehicles from any source, always provided that they meet their production and other commitments under the program. Any Canadian vehicle manufacturer who meets the requirements of the program to achieve stipulated levels of output may import duty free vehicles and original equipment parts, provided he also maintains the required ratio of output of vehicles to sales of vehicles within Canada. Indeed, it is the exercise of this right which shows that the production, employment and rationalization objects of the automotive program are being met.
Mr. Chairman, have we reverted to motions? Is there no opportunity to reply to the statement just made?

speechtext: The hon. member for Calgary South.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a few words in connection with the oil pipe line and I should also like to speak briefly about oil in Canada in general. First of all I should like to say that the decision of

the government to go along with the construction of the oil pipe line appears to be a reversal of government policy on this subject, in contrast to their policy with regard to the unification of the armed forces. The difference between the two policies is that, insofar as unification of the armed forces is concerned, the minister involved has completely ignored the advice of his experts. As a matter of fact, he has fired his experts and found another group of experts who would agree with the opinion that he holds. On the other hand I must congratulate the government for accepting the advice of their experts-the experts in this case being the National Energy Board-in connection with the oil pipe line. Many arguments, both in favour and against the construction of the pipe line, were placed before the National Energy Board which, after careful consideration, agreed to the construction of the line.
