He was pleading the case for northern Ontario, which is overlooked all too often by our industrialists, economists and government planners and is bypassed in the parade of opportunity and prosperity so prominent in parts of central Canada more fortunately placed by geography, climate and accessibility to foreign markets.
Although I sympathize with the position put forward by the hon. member for Port Arthur and his colleague the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, and though it parallels the type of argument I have previously advanced in this house on behalf of western Canada on other issues, I should like to take this opportunity to compliment the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources on the decision made regarding Trans-Canada Pipe Lines application to supply gas to the east via a United States route. I think this is a progressive, constructive and imaginative policy. I think it will be conclusively proven within a very short time of the pipe line going into operation, provided approval is granted on the other side of the border, that the new line will provide a trememdous new impetus and source of strength to the oil and gas industries of western Canada. As a consequence the entire Canadian economy will profit.

The southwestern Ontario industrial complex will benefit to an immeasurable degree by the new supply of natural gas which will be brought in to feed its booming industry. More than that, I believe that the new pipe line, if it comes into existence, will offer Canada a chance to make substantial improvements in its balance of payments position with the United States. Therefore, by all criteria I submit, and I suggest that a great many western Canadians will agree, that this policy is a great step forward and a great shot in the arm for the Canadian economy. I think the government is to be commended, and the minister highly complimented, for this imaginative policy and the imaginative, progressive decision which the minister made.
Under the terms of the agreement entered into by our government, there is no threat to Canadian sovereignty or our political or economic self-determination. In the last few days in the house critics of the decision made by the government have suggested that there is indeed an overt threat to our sovereignty and self-determination at the political and economic levels. I fail to see where this argument holds water. I fail to see where this argument can be justified, when in the precise terms of the agreement there is an airtight guarantee against encroachments upon our sovereignty, political and economic.
There is a provision in the agreement, as hon. members know, to loop the line through northern Ontario by 1970. I ask those members who have criticized the government for the stand it has taken: Where, in the terms and context of the agreement, is there any threat or loophole by which Canadian interests can be compromised? I wonder what the critics of this program want for Canada? The evidently feel it is somehow un-Canadian to pipe natural gas or any of our natural products through the United States.
The other night the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam referred to the so-called disadvantages of building this line through the United States. He said "we will lose the economic advantages, the impetus and the taxes" that would accrue from building the line through Canada. I hoped to be able to ask the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam directly about that comment today. I have not been able to do so because it has proven impossible for us both to be in the chamber at the same time. However, I will discuss this with him outside the chamber, after I put the question on the record: What does the hon. member think about the seriousness of losing
November 4, 1966

our own eastern Canadian natural gas market?
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
He talks about the serious economic advantages that we will lose by building the line through the United States, the impetus to our economy and the taxes. What about the serious loss of that huge, rich and still unmeasured eastern Canadian natural gas market for which we are in a race against time and in the capture of which we are in a narrow race against interests in the United States?
I will ask the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, and his colleagues who share his views on this subject, which is the more serious loss for Canada? I think the answer is that the more serious loss would be that huge, rich market which is still untapped, waiting to be served and waiting to fuel the economic boom of Canada in the 1970's and the 1980's. I will also ask the critics of the policy whether they feel it is uncanadian to take advantage of our surplus natural resources and commodities in order to improve our balance of payments situation with the United States. Provided that our proven and known resources are as inexhaustible as our natural resources are according to the estimates of the best professional experts, what are they for if not to make Canada stronger and richer?
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle, in discussing the situation the other night, described himself as a nationalist. At the same time he pointed out that the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam is also a nationalist. I think all of us in this house are nationalists in that we are here to do whatever we can, to build a bigger, a better, a greater and a truer united Canadian nation. However, the term "nationalism" is not necessarily a panacea for all our real and imagined ills. I think semantics are involved here. There is good nationalism and bad nationalism. The nationalism of the 18th and 19th centuries is not necessarily good nationalism in 1966. Faced as we are with the realities of life on this continent and abroad, some of the principles that were perhaps highly admirable and laudable 100 or 150 years ago are simply not practical or good nationalism in 1966. In 1966, the best nationalism is a program that will make Canada strong, rich, wealthy and able to stand on her own two feet; able to increase her gross national product and her population to the point where we do not have to be anybody's servant, assistant or satellite.
Interim Supply
We have been given, through good fortune and fate, some of the richest reserves of natural resources of all types on the face of the globe. Only now are we reaching the point where we are tapping those rich reserves. It is in the exploitation of those reserves that true Canadian wealth and strength, and therefore nationalism, lies.
In considering the application of Trans Canada Pipe Lines the National Energy Board, the government and all members of this house, will have to face the question of geography. In certain contexts and situations, even in North America, I believe that to say that the lines of communication or commerce should be contained and confined within one's own national boundaries is perfectly justifiable. However, a big part of central Canada is virtually undeveloped, unpopulated and uninhabited. If that area had been richly populated, the situation would have been different. We have to try and make a situation work in this country in which we have pockets of population widely separated, and only connected by thin lines of communication. When considering how to move our products and our people from point to point, in many cases through such forbidding terrain and forbidding climatic conditions, we must realize we cannot always have the best of both worlds.
I think there is no comparison between the pipe line situation of 1966 and that of 1956, and any attempt to equate the two is a smokescreen.
I think the minister has been painstakingly careful in protecting Canada's interests. It is my view that the enlightened decision which has been made was a result of an appreciation of the fact that Canadians are non-partisan on at least one thing, that is they want to develop the greatest industrial muscle possible for this country to enable it to emerge with real political and economic strength as well as enduring national pride. I believe that the policy being undertaken with respect to our natural gas reserves is compatible with that goal. Any other course would be narrow, restrictive and reactionary.
Mr. Chairman, before concluding my remarks I should like to say one or two things about another area of concern, that is the area of education in this country. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle referred to this subject earlier in this debate. Like many members of this house, and many other legislators across the land I was deeply disappointed by the results of the recent federal-provincial tax sharing and tax structure conference in

November 4, 1966
Interim Supply
so far as educational considerations were concerned.
We are in a criticial period, and therefore I believe that in the next few months the federal government will have to face up to its responsibilities in the educational field. I am talking here about financial support and assistance, not about interference. I would appeal for a revival of the bold scholarship and bursary program which was advanced by this government a few months ago and which now has been abandoned. I would appeal for the convening of a federal-provincial conference for the purpose of working out a constitutionally acceptable arrangement for government aid to education. We need money for teacher training and teachers' salaries. The amount being made available to the provinces, mine among them, in the next fiscal year is a pittance in comparison with what is required. Someone left that conference saying that the provinces were going home equalized in unhappiness. I think, from the point of view of responsibilities in the field of education, perhaps it would have been more appropriate to say they were going home equalized on the brink of disaster, for the crisis in education in this country is severe.
I will ask the government: What about the Deutsch and the Bladen reports? How can the government, in the face of those researched and documented conclusions, be so oblivious of the needs of the provinces in this top priority field? The federal government will have to assert itself more directly in the field of assistance for the training of our future generations and in supplying researchers and teachers. If they do not, I submit we will lose the race I talked about a few moments ago when I was speaking in economic terms of markets; we will lose our strength, identity and our Canadian self-fulfilment.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, before proceeding with the main substance of my remarks I should like to support wholeheartedly the protests from the opposition side of the house With respect to the minister's method of proceeding with the integration and unification of the armed forces. I shall have more to say about this in a later debate, but I would support their plea that the minister refer this matter to the committee on defence and allow the arguments for and against to be brought before that committee. In this way committee members will have a fuller understanding of the situation and will be

able to make a report to the house based on their inquiries, their hearing of the evidence and their deliberations.
Having said that, I support the former speakers who have dealt with the question of the government's latest agreement in connection with the Trans-Canada pipe line being looped into the United States and then brought back into Canada further on.
In that connection, Mr. Chairman, I start on a more or less philosophical basis. I am often in favour of something philosophically, but I frankly admit that when it comes to technical questions I have to rely on the opinions of experts. I intend to quote the opinions of one or two experts before I take my seat.
I was very much taken, Mr. Chairman, with this statement which was made some time ago by Professor W. L. Morton of the University of Manitoba, and I think that this is something which should be kept in mind. He said:
Canada has preserved and confirmed the essentials of the greatest of civilizations in the grimmest of environments. It is an accomplishment worthy of a better end than absorption in another and an alien society, however friendly and however strong in its own ideals. In that accomplishment and its continuance lies the relevance of Canadian history.
I think that that is the philosophy that motivates the members of this party when they take a strong position against the government's tendency to develop our natural resources, our industries and our society on the basis of continentalism.
I should also like to quote a short extract taken from the April 1964 issue of "Engineering and Contract Record":
The federal government must re-assert its clear obligation to frame national development policy for the best future of all Canadians. This requires urgent action to restate our historic policy of east-west sharing of wealth.
Speeches by present government leaders advocating integration of resources with the U.S. and massive exports of water threaten the economic independence of the country. Some sort of national policy on resource development is needed, but it should place Canada's national interests before any export plans.
The members of this group, Mr. Chairman, support that point of view.
This is the third occasion on which I have had the opportunity of speaking in this house in opposition to the government's policy of the day. The first time was on the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines bill. We failed to make this company into a public utility and lent a very wealthy corporation, if I remember correctly, $80 million to invest in this pipe line.
November 4, 1966

We lent this money at a very reasonable rate of interest. We then allowed them to pay off the loan and to reap all the benefits of this very profitable pipe line. It is also to be remembered that we built the eastern half of the line at our own expense. This situation created a very interesting debate in this house which led, without any question, to the defeat of the Liberal government in 1957. The Canadian people at that time grasped what was going on with respect to the development of this pipe line.

As my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre says, together with a $6 increase in the old age pension. I give him credit; he is never far away from the old age pensioners and he has reminded me of that so that I would repeat it once more. And it is quite correct.
He follows us on this.

The next unfortunate demonstration of continentalism, Mr. Chairman, was when this government signed the Columbia River treaty after the Prime Minister had made speeches against the treaty which had been introduced by the former government, and after my hon. friend for Coast-Capilano had written articles in the Vancouver papers condemning the treaty. There, again, was an illustration of the somewhat differing points of view of the government, the members of this party and some other members of the opposition.
The treaty was opposed at that time, as we all know, by the late General McNaughton, some 30 to 40 well informed engineers, by trade unions in British Columbia, by farmers organizations, by the New Democratic Party and a number of other well informed persons, including Mr. James G. Ripley, editor of the "Engineering and Contract Record" and Mr. Larratt Higgins, the economic consultant for the Ontario Hydro.
Time is proving that these people were correct, Mr. Chairman. I shall never forget in the committee asking Mr. Williston if allowance were made for all contingencies, whether there would be ample money to build these dams. He assured the committee that there would be. There would be $55 million left over which would go toward the construction of the generators at the Mica Creek dam. We all know that things are turning out a little differently now.

In that connection, Mr. Chairman, I want to place on the record a letter received by the Minister of Finance from Mr. W. A. C. Bennett, the premier and minister of finance of the government of British Columbia. I have been asked to do this by a number of people in British Columbia who have not been able to get a copy of this letter. I do wish to make a comment on it. It is dated September 16, 1966, addressed from Victoria and reads as follows:
Dear Mr. Sharp:
At the Tax Structure Committee meeting held in Ottawa September 14 and 15 I submitted certain specific fiscal requests on behalf of the people of British Columbia.
In order that there may be no misunderstanding about these matters I would like to detail the requests for your consideration.
1.	$19,747,500 requested for construction subsidies for the provincially owned Pacific Great Eastern Railway.
We all know what the premier of British Columbia said about the profitable Pacific Great Eastern Railway in the past.
2.	appropriate sharing under the Trans-Canada Highway agreement for the Second Narrows bridge at Vancouver. Originally built at a cost of 24.2 million it is agreed that tolls collected reduce the shareable cost to $21.8 million.
3.	$30 million requested on behalf of the British Columbia Hydro and Power Authority resulting from increased costs of the Columbia River dams due to the imposition of the 11 per cent federal sales tax after the signing of the agreement.
I asked the Prime Minister in the house whether this sales tax was in effect when the government of British Columbia signed the agreement with the government of Canada respecting the construction of the Columbia River treaty dams, and the Prime Minister said yes. It was in fact in effect months before. Premier Bennett signed that agreement but did not know that this sales tax was in effect. Some of his senior officials at least must have known so that that statement is entirely inaccurate. Then he goes on:

4.	Government of Canada credit to be made available to the British Columbia Hydro & Power Authority for its large capital construction programs. In such instances the government of the province of British Columbia would be prepared to guarantee any borrowings involved.
I am informed that the sum first suggested approached $100 million. He continues:
These are matters that vitally concern the citizens of this province and your early attention to their implementation would be appreciated.
Yours very truly,
W. A. C. Bennett,
Premier and Minister of Finance

That is a very different story from the one the premier was telling at the time of the provincial campaign.
Would the hon. member permit a question? Does he support the recommendations contained in the letter he has just read?
I beg your pardon?
Do you support the submissions contained in the letter you have just read from the premier of our province of British Columbia?

I have to know more of the background behind this request. I shall have to make a further study of the situation before coming to a conclusion. Like the Secretary of State for External Affairs, I am giving the matter serious consideration. However, Premier Bennett has said British Columbia is free of direct debt.
I quote from the Financial Times of October 24 to demonstrate, shall I say, the unfortunate path we have pursued in being willing to approach these questions in the first place from a continental point of view. The article is entitled: "Bennett Reassuring, But Hydro Financing Doubts Remain". It reads as follows:
The Columbia scheme cost, with completion by 1973, was put at $410 million. The 1966 program calls for a total investment of some $321 million-a significant portion of the vaunted "B.C. boom."
Here are some of the factors which have given rise to doubts about the financing of the power projects:
On Feb. 15, Mr. Bennett appeared to reject Liberal urgings that he ask for federal aid for the projects.
I presume those were Liberal urgings in the provincial house, not in this house. Continuing:
Two days later, B.C. Hydro announced it had applied for a $75 million loan from the Canada Pension Plan investment fund to help with the 1966 $300 million program.
In April, a $25 million Hydro bond issue with a coupon rate of 5.75% got a sluggish reception on the market.
In May, Mr. Bennett reported after a visit to New York that B.C. Hydro could raise $100 million on Wall Street in the immediate future.
In June, he announced the underwriting of a $50 million U.S. issue. It is not yet clear whether this was a first instalment or a forced cutback in the $100 million forecast.
The N.D.P. opposition produced figures to support its claim that an extra $200 million would be needed to complete the projects on schedule.
That was in reference to the Columbia treaty projects. The article goes on:

B.C. Hydro's profit slumped 40% from the previous year, from $13.1 million to $7.5 million. Dr. Gordon Shrum, Hydro co-chairman, conceded that labour costs on the Peace project would rise by $25 million by 1968.
The article concludes with these words:
After winning the election, the premier embarked on his widespread program of spending restraint, and asked Ottawa for help with his cherished power projects.
I mention this to indicate the fact that those who were opposed to this project in the first instance are being proven correct every day, regardless of the article I read in the Financial Post written by Dr. Keenleyside, co-chairman of the B.C. Hydro and Power Authority, who said that there was a certain fluidity in the situation, whatever that means, and that this was the finest agreement ever signed by any government in Canada in all Canadian history with respect to the development of water resources.
At the same time I might mention that we have received nothing for the value of water used for irrigation, domestic or industrial purposes. I have seen figures published in California indicating that on this basis alone, on the basis of what this water is being sold for in the areas concerned, we should have been entitled to an additional $40 million annually at least for the use of the water for the purposes I have mentioned. I mention these facts to indicate that on two major occasions, in our opinion, we have taken the wrong direction.
I now want to deal with the pipe line debate. I must say that I do not feel competent to deal with the technical aspects of this question, but I will say frankly that I am convinced we should develop our natural resources in Canada, keeping in mind the needs of the Canadian people in this and following generations. To that extent I might be accused of being somewhat prejudiced in favour of my country.
I have here an article written by Mr. James G. Ripley who is a professional engineer and editor of the Engineering and Contract Record. The same gentleman wrote a very interesting article about the development of the Columbia river. That article was entitled:	"The Columbia River Scandal".
Numerous statements in this article are being proven correct as time goes on. Because of that I am inclined to listen to his arguments. He has a very interesting article in this issue which he wrote after the government had rejected the recommendations of the National Energy Board. The headline reads: "The
November 4, 1966

Pipeline Stays In Canada." The body of the article reads as follows:
In spite of the hysteria it caused in the gas industry, the federal cabinet's veto of Trans-Canada Pipelines' plan to build its second transcontinental line through the United States was based on sound analysis of economic facts and is a good decision for Canada.
Trans-Canada wanted to service its rapidly growing eastern Canadian markets by building a 989-mile pipe line through the U.S. from Emerson, Man., to Sarnia, Ont., is a 50 per cent partnership with a U.S. firm. The cabinet veto means that the new line likely will go through northern Ontario, along the line of the first pipe line, built during the fifties after a controversy similar to, though much more violent, than the present debate.
At first glance, the cabinet appeared to have ignored the work of the National Energy Board, which had approved the U.S. plan only a few weeks earlier. However, a closer analysis shows that the two decisions follow a logical sequence from one jurisdiction to a higher one, and are not really in conflict. Nevertheless, the cabinet move was unexpected, and it stirred the wrath of western gas producers and eastern distributors, who accused the Prime Minister of letting emotional nationalism prevail over economic facts. But they are wrong. The economic facts and the national interest both favour an all-Canadian line. The decision was the only proper one a Canadian prime minister could make.
Even the N.E.B. gave its approval to the U.S. plan with serious reservations. The board accepted the plan because it was the only detailed proposal submitted and because it offered a quick solution to an immediate problem of supplying gas to a market where shortages are imminent. But in its well-reasoned report to the government the board virtually wrote in its own dissenting opinion, which includes compelling reasons for looping the line in Canada. The report effectively demolishes several of the major arguments of the continentalists who have led Canada perilously close to the point of no return in economic integration with the United States.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
Of course, after writing this editorial he was very disappointed by the change in the government's decision. He goes on to give the case for the United States plan at some length and, I think, with technical ability. I might say that this gentleman consulted other engineers. He is very careful when writing these articles. I know that when he was dealing with the Columbia river treaty he got opinions from groups of engineers. Some 29 or 30 engineers agreed with the opinion he expressed at that time. He is very careful in getting the facts on which he comes to a conclusion, and this is why he says the original decision of the government was the correct one.
I quote from his article as follows:
If the costs of the two alternatives are comparable and the effects on domestic gas markets and exports are not significantly different, the additional
Interim Supply
advantages of the all-Canadian route make it clearly the correct choice for Canada.
To start with, control of the system would remain with Canada, whereas the U.S. line would be regulated by the U.S. Federal Power Commission. A sobering preview of what the latter alternative could mean is contained in a current F.P.C. staff report on the Trans-Canada application. The report states bluntly that the commission couldn't care less about reducing gas prices in eastern Canada, and that its sole objective (as required by U.S. law) is to serve the best interests of the United States. The American section of the line would also be 50 per cent owned by a U.S. company and this would mean that operating decisions would both be cumbersome to make and would end up as compromises between U.S. and Canadian requirements. Trans-Canada's claim that the U.S. route would protect Canadian interests is not valid, compared with the alternative of a line 100 per cent owned and regulated in Canada.
Second, the difference to Canadian development, the so-called multiplier factor, is immense. The northern line would use pipe with 90 per cent Canadian content and $1 billion worth of construction and development would go to Canadian contractors. Also, at the end of the financing period, we would own this great asset outright.
Canada must continue to develop economically by closer east-west communication and the stimulus of the new pipe line through northern Ontario would add immeasurably to the depth of what is now the weakest link in the narrow transcontinental Canadian civilization.
Some critics have expressed fears that Mr. Pearson's reversal of the N.E.B. recommendation will damage the prestige of that board. It's hard to see why. In fact, the prestige of the board should even be enhanced. The board made an excellent technical analysis and no one has questioned its findings. The cabinet recognized the closeness of the technical comparisons and chose the Canadian route for reasons that were, by its own admission, beyond the board's jurisdiction. Had Mr. Pearson vetoed the U.S. scheme before the N.E.B. study, he could rightly have been accused of making an irrational choice. But he waited until the facts were in, and then made the final decision, that only a national government could make, considering the total effect on the entire country, now and in the future.
Let us hope there will be no reversal of this decision by a government which has a reputation for second-guessing itself. If there is, the government can expect an all-out parliamentary attack by Mr. Diefenbaker, a man who upset a previous Liberal government on the pipe line issue and who knows from memory the entire script of pipe line debate. But a more important reason for the government to stick to its decision is that it is right for Canada. That should be enough.
This article was written by James G. Ripley, but since it appeared the government has reassessed the situation and reversed its decision.
I must confess that I do not get a great deal of correspondence on a matter of this type which more seriously affects Ontario and eastern Canada but I have had engineers write me on this question expressing their

November 4, 1966
Interim Supply
serious concern that the government has decided to reverse its decision. I hope that as a result of the concern that has been expressed by many hon. members on the opposition side of the chamber, and by a few members on the government side, the government will find valid reasons to reverse its decision once more before this debate is terminated.

Mr. Chairman, earlier in the week I made a few introductory remarks on national defence and at that time promised the minister I would give him chapter and verse with regard to his concealment of the facts and his misleading of the House of Commons and the people of Canada. That is what I propose to do today. It will involve reading certain excerpts from Hansard and from newspaper articles, and if subsequent material needs to be supplied I may enlarge on my remarks next week.
Through a program of surreptitious activity and concealment of facts and through misleading statements, the minister has left the Canadian people in a state of very great confusion with regard to national defence. Recently he has been assisted by what seems to me to be a conspiracy of silence on the part of our nationally owned broadcasting corporation which has omitted to mention anything that has transpired in the House of Commons this week either on its eight o'clock news broadcast in the morning or its eleven o'clock television news at night, which are the only times I have a chance to hear what is being broadcast by the C.B.C. If there is such a conspiracy, then all I can say is that we shall have to continue our efforts until we break through this silent treatment.
I know that the minister and his friends are counting on the apathy and indifference of the Canadian people, but if there are apathy and indifference on their part with regard to national defence the reason for it rests with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. We have no control over the C.B.C. We do not exercise control over it in the House of Commons but we provide the money for it. But neither do we have control over the press of this country, which has done a far better job of conveying to the people what is going on in the house. The C.B.C. costs the taxpayers of this country $100 million a year but, as I say, it appears to have entered into a conspiracy of silence with regard to this issue at a time when we are facing a crisis in national defence.
Over the last three years the minister has confused the Canadian people and the House
[Mr. Herrldge.l
of Commons through his failure to give adequate information. The extent of that confusion is brought forcibly to our attention by an editorial in the last issue of The Legionary, the national magazine of the Royal Canadian Legion. This editorial has been quoted previously, and I want to refer only to two paragraphs. It is headed, "Integration and Unification-Legion Requests Full, Clear-cut Information". I quote:
We are, however, deeply concerned about the question of the state and condition of our defence forces at any given time. It appears to us that sufficient thought and planning have not been given to the important questions of tradition, morale and esprit de corps or, if so, the members of Canada's forces and the public have certainly been kept in ignorance.
I wish I could underline in Hansard those last few words: "The public have certainly been kept in ignorance."
The Royal Canadian Legion urges your government to make clear, without further delay, the detailed plans connected with the integration, and particularly the proposed unification of the forces so that the judgment made by Canadian organizations and citizens will be based on frank and comprehensive official information and fact, not on rumour and supposition, as seems to be largely the case at the present time.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I have been a member of the Royal Canadian Legion since 1927 and I regret to say to my comrades in that organization that their activity is too little and too late. That is a phrase with which they are familiar from the period just before the second world war. We have debated the question of national defence in this house during 1963, 1964, 1965 and 1966. During this period we have tried to get information on this subject from the minister. We have seen him pursue a course of destroying the armed forces and their identity. It is only now that people are awakening to the fact that what we were pointing out in those years is just about upon us and will become established if the minister is allowed to have his way. So I hope that the Royal Canadian Legion will pursue its investigation immediately, or by Christmas time or early in the New Year they will find that the Canadian defence forces have no resemblance whatsoever to the Royal Canadian Navy, the Royal Canadian Air Force or the Canadian Army as they used to know these services. Fortunately those bodies still are in existence at the present time.
Other members who have spoken have read editorials which have indicated the confusion and misunderstanding on the part of the public with regard to these topics. Why
November 4, 1966

should the public and members of this House of Commons not be confused? This afternoon the hon. member for Megantic, one of the most alert members of the House of Commons and one who has been a member of the defence committee, said that he does not know what has been going on. He said that the minister was clouding the issue. He said, "Nobody seems to know what is going on". This is said from a member of the House of Commons who is alert, intelligent and well informed on most subjects. He says he has not been given full information. Newspaper editorials across the country have indicated the same thing. It is no wonder that the people have not had accurate information. I should like to quote now from the Ottawa Citizen of July 26. This is a statement by the Minister of National Defence; these are his own words:
Two years of carrying out integration policies have already resulted in cost-cutting of $143 million. I am convinced the savings will be even more substantial when the process is completed-in the vicinity of $150 million a year.
I say to you, Mr. Chairman, that that is misleading information. It was only a few days ago, on October 31, that the minister, to paraphrase his own words, said that there had been a drop of 20,000, in the number of people employed in the armed services and he raised the figure to 23,000 civilians and servicemen. He said at page 9350 of Hansard:
If we still had these additional 23,000 people to pay next year at current rates I would say we should have to find at least $150 million more in our budget than we will be asking for in present circumstances.
That, sir, is a complete refutation of the statement he made in the Ottawa Citizen on July 26 when he said that the saving was a result of integration. The fact is that the cost cut has resulted from a reduction in the strength of our forces. His statement to the Citizen was misleading. Whether it was deliberate or not I do not know. The minister is not here for me to ask him. If he cannot stand the heat he gets out of the kitchen, but I am not going to be inhibited in speaking my mind just because the minister happens to be absent. In fact, he has a habit of attacking people who are not members of the House of Commons and cannot answer him here. If anyone would like to send for the minister, I have one or two questions to ask him.

our naval forces. Frequently he has talked about that. He said that they are superior to what they ever have been before in peacetime. This statement was refuted by the hon. member for Calgary North. It has been refuted by Admiral Landymore's testimony. Admiral Landymore has shown that although we have the ships and are getting ships and although we have the armament and the new devices for anti-submarine detection, we do not have the men to man the ships. This is what the minister said on October 31 at page 9350 of Hansard:
I state it as an incontrovertible fact. The antisubmarine capacity of the navy today is greater than it has ever been in peacetime and I will stand by that because I can prove it to the satisfaction of anybody who is willing to look at the facts.
Those are the words of the minister. Everything hinges on that word "capacity". I do not doubt for one minute that the ships are better, that the sonar devices are better than we had in the past, and that the detection apparatus is better for the anti-submarine role, but to tell the public that the anti-submarine capacity, or capability as he sometimes refers to it, of the navy is greater than it has been at any other time in peacetime is not accurate. We can have the ships but if we do not man them we have no capacity for carrying out an anti-submarine capability.
Admiral Landymore has pointed out that we are short 2,600 men with the present complement of ships, or 1,500 if some of the ships are decommissioned, and that by next spring, unless there is an immediate upsurge in recruiting for the navy, our complement of ships which can be put to sea and be active will be reduced until we have about 12 or 13. Yet the minister releases to the public the information that our navy has a greater antisubmarine capacity or capability than at any other time in peacetime. That is an inaccurate statement. Is it intended to be deliberately misleading? That is what I should like to ask the minister.
Now, sir, let me give you another example. As found in the Globe and Mail for Saturday, July 16, the minister, when replying to the hon. member for Calgary North who had suggested a royal commission, used these words:
This is unnecessary and would be a waste of taxpayers' money. The standing committee on national defence has thoroughly investigated all aspects of defence organization.
That is an inaccurate statement. The committee on national defence has not been given
957G

November 4, 1966
Interim Supply
the opportunity to investigate thoroughly all aspects of defence organization. In the last few days we have had an exposure of evidence which was suppressed and not permitted to be presented to that committee. So, again you have an inaccurate and misleading statement by this Minister of National Defence. In the same issue of the same paper I should like to read the following words of the minister:
Long ago I called my commanders together and asked them if they could support my policies. They were given the opportunity of dissenting. I told them I respected their rights to disagree and I made it clear that they could leave with full honours. None did.
o (4:30 p.m.)
The minister admitted publicly that he did call his senior officers together and he did say, to put is in ordinary phraseology, either you go along with my policies or get out. He then said, according to this public statement, that none did get out. Yet we have before us evidence galore which shows that a number of senior officers were either fired or accepted early retirement because they could not go along with those policies. That is another inaccurate statement by the Minister of National Defence.
As far back as 1964 we discussed the question of integration and unification. We have now had a new word, amalgamation, and I suggest there is still another, fusion, which could be followed perhaps by confusion. That represents the policy of this minister.
In 1964 we discussed these problems. At page 5085 of Hansard for that year-I well remember the difficulties we had with the minister at that time-he said in answer to the hon. member for Calgary North:
X would like to repeat for my hon. friend for Calgary North something that I had thought would be self-evident to everyone, but which apparently is not. That is, we will still have, as I have said before, squadrons of ships, squadrons of planes, battalions of men, and it does not matter whether these are in three services or one in so far as their operational effectiveness is concerned-
He used those terms, "squadrons of ships, squadrons of planes, battalions of men" and he left the impression that there would be no susbtantial change and that we would still have an identifiable navy and an identifiable air force. Was that done deliberately or through stupidity?
On July 4 of the same year I entered into the debate and said, as recorded at pages 5114 and 5115 of Hansard:
In the second place we have asked him to explain what he means with regard to unification and

integration of the services. Does he intend to wipe out our three fighting services and attempt to make one out of them?
I then said:
What we fail to understand is why the minister, as a responsible minister of the crown, will not give answers to these questions. He sits silent with regard to the unification of the services. He has told us at other times, or his words lend themselves to this interpretation, that he intends to have just one service.
At the end of that paragraph I said:
But what does the minister mean? Is he wiping out the infantry regiments and the tank regiments which have a tradition behind them going back almost a hundred years?
No.
Is he retaining the highland regiments, for example? Why cannot he answer that simple question?
I already have.

Is he retaining the artillery regiment or is he wiping it out? What about the engineers? Then where does the air force come in, and the navy? Are these men all to be in the same service or is there some misunderstanding of what the minister has been saying? I submit these are fair and reasonable questions ... I make one final request to the Minister of National Defence. Let us have the answers.
That was as fair and as reasonable a request as I could make under the circumstances. We received no answer from the minister. We pursued these problems at different times. I will not give all the references, but on February 21, 1966, the subject of unification came up. Let us see how far we got that time. We were debating the final supplementary estimates and I said, as recorded at page 1573 of Hansard of that date:
The minister has not dealt with the subject of unification. Is there anyone in the country who knows what he means by unification? He has never answered that question.
At page 1598 of Hansard for the same year the hon. member for Acadia said:
Would the minister permit a question in respect of unification? Would he answer the question of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre last night? What does he mean by unification? Does he mean one force, one uniform? Would he explain this more fully?
Unification means one force. I think this is understood.
One uniform too?

I think my hon. friend will agree there can never be one uniform that would cover all situations.
There we have a confusing situation. We are to have squadrons of aircraft, squadrons of ships, regiments, all without the loss of any identity. Will there be one uniform? The minister says there could not be one because
November 4, 1966



one would not cover all situations. That is the state in which the minister has left the matter time after time in spite of our efforts.
In a newspaper article there was a suggestion that Admiral O'Brien, appointed to the maritime command, had been given the assurance that the identity of the navy would not be disturbed until parliament had decided the issue. Headline writers do not have much space but the headline on this article which appeared in the Globe and Mail on July 21 reads:	"O'Brien Says Ottawa Gave Him
Assurance On Service Identities". When you read the article you find that it was only a temporary assurance, but the public reads the headlines and would think that the services' identities would be retained. On September 9 I asked this question, as recorded in Hansard at page 8253:
I have a question for the Minister of National Defence based on a statement he made in the House of Commons on May 12, 1964, appearing in Hansard at page 3188:	"There will, of course,
always be soldiers, sailors and airmen." I ask the minister if those words, "soldiers, sailors and airmen" as designating the different fighting components of the armed forces will be officially retained in the new model force which he is creating?
The minister then replied:
As I made very clear at that time, any force with the responsibilities which our forces now have and will continue to have in the years ahead will require soldiers, sailors and airmen trained in their particular professioinal capacities.
Then I asked him this question:
Will the soldiers, sailors and airmen in the new model force continue to wear uniforms of the style and colour so long familiar as distinguishing each branch of the service?
The minister then replied:
This is not the kind of urgent question which, under the rules, is ordinarily answered on the orders of the day.
Anyone who can get answers from the Minister of National Defence must be a superior human being, and I do not fall within that category. I found out, however, from the Ottawa Citizen of July 25, 1965, that a statement was issued by Rear Admiral William Landymore, retired, that he was informed in the spring of 1965.
Mr. Hellyer announced to us that he intended to implement a single walking-out dress and rank structure by July, 1967.
That information has never been given to the House of Commons by this minister. When I asked him the question which I just read on September 9 he brushed me aside by saying it was not the type of question that
Interim Supply
should be asked on orders of the day. One of his senior officers in 1965, a year and a half ago, knew that the minister intended to have a single walking-out dress and rank structure by July, 1967. He concealed that information from the House of Commons; he concealed it from the public. How can you place any reliance on a minister who does that? These are instances of misleading statements. I now come to a misleading statement made on August 30, 1966, when the hon. member for Vancouver East asked this question of the minister:
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
Would the minister inform this house whether in respect of officers of the armed services giving evidence before the defence committee of the House of Commons it is correct that their presentations are received by him and censored before they are allowed to be made to the committee of the House of Commons?
The minister replied:
No, Mr. Speaker.
In other words, he said that he did not receive the presentations that people were going to make to the defence committee. Yet just the other day he admitted in the house that the senior officers who were to make presentations to the defence committee appeared before him or the associate minister with their presentations, which were reviewed. Was the statement of the minister that I have just read to the committee intended to mislead the House of Commons? It certainly did mislead the House of Commons because we thought he had not received Admiral Landymore and looked at his brief or had it reviewed before the evidence was given to the defence committee. Let me give you, sir, another example of a misleading statement. On October 27, as reported at page 9165 of Hansard, I asked this question of the minister:
Has the minister authorized one walking-out uniform similar in pattern, style and colour for all members of the armed forces?
The minister replied:
Not yet, Mr. Speaker.
Then we went on to talk about the walking-out uniform, and I asked:
Will the minister give a clear indication of what is government policy in this respect-
I was referring to a single walking-out uniform for the armed forces. The minister replied:
It was set out in the white paper in 1964.

November 4, 1966
Interim Supply
I said that it was not set out in the white paper, and I rose on a question of privilege and used these words:
We now have the Minister of National Defence saying that the program to establish a single uniform for all members of the armed forces was set out in the white paper in 1964. This, sir, is not true. Evasive and misleading answers are being given by this minister. I challenge him to substantiate his statement.
He did not substantiate it, and I say he misled the House of Commons with regard to that matter.
The minister has now reversed his policy as shown in the white paper. In the white paper there are three references to Canada's obligations. They are set out as follows:
The objectives of Canadian policy, which cannot be dissociated from foreign policy, are to preserve the peace by supporting collective defence measures to deter military aggression; to support Canadian foreign policy including that arising out of our participation in international organizations, and to provide for the protection and surveillance of our territory, our air-space and our coastal waters.
On the next page of the white paper those three objectives are repeated but in a somewhat different order. The first one is:
Collective measures for maintenance of peace and security as embodied in the charter of the United Nations, including the search for balanced and controlled disarmament;
The second is:
Collective defence as embodied in the North Atlantic Treaty;
The third is:
Partnership with the United States in the defence of North America;
Then, fourth and last is this objective:
National measures to discharge responsibility for the security and protection of Canada.
Then we find in the white paper a section on priorities on page 24. The priorities, to which we paid attention, are listed in this way:
1.	Forces for the direct protection of Canada which can be deployed as required.
2.	Forces-in-being as part of the deterrent in the European theatre.
3.	Maritime forces-in-being as a contribution to the deterrent.
4.	Forces-in-being for U.N. peace-keeping operations-
The minister has now reversed what he said in the white paper. He has put the United Nations peace-keeping operations at the top of the list; he is going to scrap the navy and air force as we have known them, make the navy just a transport vehicle for
I Mr. Churchill.]
army troops, and similarly with the air force. What is he doing about the defence of Canada, the defence of our coastal waters, forces-in-being for the defence of our land mass, and forces for use in the air? This is where the minister has seriously misled the people of this country and has reversed his policy.
Time and time again the minister has asked us to read the white paper, and time and time again I have read it. The only thing in the white paper upon which the minister can rely is the statement that he was going to form a single, unified force. But everybody in the country thought he meant a unified command, an integration of the support facilities below, and that we would have what we had in wartime, combined operations. All the time the minister meant that he was going to put all the forces together, fuse them, amalgamate them and put them in one uniform. He did not give that information to this House of Commons. I say to you, sir, that he misled this House of Commons, and if he were in his seat at the present moment I would say that he knowingly and deliberately misled the house.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word or two on this supply motion and in particular about the Minister of National Defence and his actions in connection with the whole question of unification and integration. I am following the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, and for this reason what I have to say will have nothing of the strength of the argument that he put forward. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre dealt very fully with the confusion that exists in regard to this question. He proved how the minister has confused the house on the question of unification, and that this confusion began two or three years ago.
This brings to mind the first impression I formed of the Minister of National Defence when I served on the defence committee a number of years ago. I remember attending a confidential luncheon at which the minister made some rather frank statements. He followed them by saying, "Whatever I say at this particular meeting I do not want you to repeat outside. But if you do repeat it outside, I will of course deny making the statements, so you will be no further ahead." As far as I know, none of the statements made at that time was repeated outside.
November 4, 196G



I formed the impression then that the minister was being very frank in making statements which certainly clarified and explained some of the actions he took while a member on this side of the house. I thought then that if he continued in that frank way the defence committee could serve a very useful purpose. But I was soon disillusioned in regard to the initial impression I gained of the minister. Now, of course, the minister, rather than being frank and honest with members of the defence committee and the house, has been, if anything, the direct opposite. He has slid around, hidden and brushed under the rug just about any and every question he has been asked in the last two years. This is evident from some of the questions read to the committee by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre and the answers received to those questions.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
It is also interesting to note that on the question of unification the Associate Minister of National Defence was also confused. He said so himself to the house when he made a speech on the interim supply motion. He wondered, he stopped and he took a second look. He consulted the experts and he reassured himself. Mr. Chairman, in a sense this is all members of the House of Commons are asking. We are asking for the privilege to consult the experts so as to reassure ourselves before we proceed with the defence legislation which the minister introduced in the house yesterday. We are asking that the government give us the same opportunity and let us consult the known experts. We wish to reassure ourselves. We are all supposedly working for the good of the whole of Canada but some of us are working in doubt. Even the associate minister said he was in doubt. He paused, he hesitated, and once again he consulted a list of experts. Why can we not all do this? Is this asking too much?
The Minister of National Defence said we can call in all kinds of witnesses but only after we have approved in principle the bill he has presented to the house on the amalgamation of the three forces. Surely everybody understands that once we do this the door will be closed and we will not be able to reverse our decision. If evidence were presented to us which caused our doubts to grow to real fear that unification is the wrong step to take, then we could not reverse our decision and all we could do would be to drop the bill completely. However, in view of the single-mindedness of purpose which the
Interim Supply
Minister of National Defence has shown in the past few months I doubt very much, even if all the members of the defence committee reached the conclusion that unification was the wrong step, that they would be able to convince him.
I am pleased to see the Associate Minister of National Defence here although I would prefer to see the Minister of National Defence present. Surely the associate minister understands the concern which members of the house feel, because he himself felt the same concern. Two years ago we were told in the white paper on defence that this measure was advisedly taken in times of peace for the purpose of promoting a more efficient and flexible fighting force for less money. What has been the case? It has not cost us less money; it has cost us more money. Have we got more for the money? No, we have not. The services are depleted and we do not have enough men to man the ships. We have hardly enough men to fly the planes, and we are diminishing our regiments.
Last night a question was raised by the hon. member for Kamloops. He put it very well but I think it needs to be repeated and answered. The question is: What are the rights of parliament in this situation? Does the minister have the right to tamper with evidence? The minister himself says he does not. Last night he told us the following, as recorded on page 9515 of Hansard:
There can be no restriction placed on the questions the committee wishes to ask witnesses, nor would I attempt in any way under any circumstances to restrict or alter what those witnesses might wish to say.
This is his firm opinion to which he now adheres. But what has been done in the past? He makes no bones about it. An official in his department tampered with, altered and changed evidence which was to be presented to that committee. Naturally, being the minister in charge of that department, he must take full responsibility for it. Even if nothing else has been accomplished, we at least have a declaration now by the minister that henceforth he will not alter evidence or restrict any witness from saying whatever he wishes to say before a committee.
The only conclusion I can draw from the minister's admission is that he now realizes he was wrong in the first instance and did not have the right to interfere, tamper with and change the evidence which a witness wished to present to the committee.

But he has achieved his purpose.
9588	COMMONS
Combines Investigation Act

He did change, hide and conceal the tacts. The house will have to deal with this serious breach of parliamentary procedure. I know of no better way to deal with it than to have the whole question submitted to the committee on privileges and elections to consider whether any minister has the right to alter, tamper with or change evidence or restrict a subordinate officer in his department from saying what he may wish to say before a committee. This is a matter of grave importance because over the past few years parliamentary committees have tried to play an important part in the democratic process of this house. This house sets up parliamentary committees for the study of particular matters and they operate under the same rules as the house. If witnesses were to appear before the House of Commons and their evidence were restricted and tampered with, I am sure the Speaker and members of the house would object to it strongly. Yet we see it being done in committees.
Last night the minister held up his hands and said he will not do it again, he will not restrict or alter evidence. But it has already been done, and all we on this side of the house can do is to ask that either the defence committee be reconvened to re-examine the witness whose evidence was tampered with and altered or that the committee on privileges and elections be called to examine whether or not a minister has the right to restrict witnesses called before a parliamentary committee. Mr. Chairman, it is five o'clock.
Progress reported.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I propose this bill because of my belief that the law must in fact treat all people equally. It is not uncommon when looking at an Ottawa newspaper, a newspaper in my own city of Winnipeg, or the newspapers in Toronto or Vancouver, to
[Mr. Nugent.l
DEBATES	November 4, 1966
find almost every day a report from the magistrates' court concerning some citizen who has been convicted of the crime of theft of a relatively small amount of money or perhaps groceries from a supermarket. If it is a first offence and the magistrate is feeling in a particularly virtuous mood, the accused may be lucky and be given a suspended sentence. If it is a second offence the magistrate will certainly send the person to prison. If it is a third offence then he is likely to go to one of our federal penitentiaries.
The law, Mr. Speaker, does not always deal with people in the same way. We have had anti-combines legislation in Canada for the past 40 or more years. This is legislation which, according to spokesmen for the Liberal party, is among the most important ever enacted in Canadian law. There is a host of cases against some of our most prominent companies in this country, companies which not once but two, three or four times have been found guilty of violating the anti-combines law. Yet not once in the history of the country has one single director, president or management representative of such a company been sent to prison, regardless of the fact that the company concerned, and I will come back to this, has violated the law on more than one occasion.
I want to deal with another type of so-called crime with which our courts have had to deal within the past year. I am glad that the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Turner) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) are in the house, because I suggest that what I am going to speak about falls within their spheres of interest. Before dealing with how the courts treat people who violate our anticombines law, I want to speak for a few moments about how the courts during the past year have treated trade unionists, labour representatives, who have been found guilty of the crime of ignoring court injunctions prohibiting picketing.
In the recent Lenkurt Electric case in Vancouver, the city from which the Minister of Labour comes, Mr. Justice Macdonald sentenced 22 persons to prison. The secretary of the Vancouver and district labour council. Patrick Neale, and the vice president of one of the locals of the International Woodworkers of America were given six months each. The former business agent of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers was sentenced to four months, and the president of the marine workers and boiler-makers union was sentenced to three months.
November 4, 1966	COMMONS DEBATES
In the Tilco case at Peterborough 22 labour leaders were sent to prison. Chief Justice Gale, in sentencing these people, explained why he was sentencing them to jail, and it is interesting to note what he said. I want to read two paragraphs from his judgment as it was reported in the Toronto Star for June 28, 1966:
I am deeply conscious of my responsibility in this matter. I must endeavour to be fair to the respondents and yet it is incumbent upon me to apply and to enforce the law, for, despite some often irresponsible, but more often unpremeditated and illogical statements and comments that apparently have been made since the release of my judgment in this case, my role as a judge is to ensure continuity for the rule of law and to thereby aid in the preservation of freedom not for some only but for all citizens.
I could not agree more with what Chief Justice Gale purports to do in bringing down his judgment.
The Toronto Globe and Mail of October 4, 1966 had an editorial entitled "No Privileged Law-breakers", from which I quote briefly:
In the Tilco case in Ontario and now in the Lenkurt case in British Columbia, the courts have at last begun to treat labour offenders as though they were just like any other offenders and subject to the same penalties.
The Toronto Star for June 28, 1966 contained an editorial entitled "Defying The Courts Won't Win Labour's Battles", and reading in part as follows:
It is certainly proper to ask whether Mr. Justice Gale could not have achieved his point, vindicated the court's authority and deterred further offences, by lighter sentences. The men involved were respectable citizens and no violence was involved.
But once the men set out to deliberately defy the courts, punishment was inevitable and, in fact, an essential part of the protest itself.
I place that on the record, Mr. Speaker, because I want to compare the attitude of the courts in these two labour cases and the attitude of the two newspapers to which I have referred, which are representative of most newspapers in Canada, with the attitude of the courts in dealing with companies convicted of violating anti-combines legislation.
Companies are directed by individuals. They are not inanimate objects which do things automatically. Somebody in the company, be he the president, the managing director or the executive vice president, must give to the company the directive that it shall get together with its so-called competitors and conspire with them to set prices which are higher than they ought to be in a competitive market, prices which have as their intention the successful milking of the public.
Combines Investigation Act
Some months ago I asked a series of questions of the minister responsible concerning how many prosecutions there had been in this regard over the past ten years, what were the names of the companies which were found guilty when prosecuted, what were the costs to the government of investigation and prosecution of the cases, and what were the penalties imposed by the courts. The questions were answered on June 27, 1966, taking up eight pages of Hansard.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
From 1956 to 1965 dozens of companies were charged, prosecuted and convicted. If you look at the list, it is a who's who of Canadian business. The biggest companies are there. Let me give a few of them: Bathurst Power and Paper Company, the Gair Company, Hinde and Dauche and St. Lawrence Corporation Limited. I could go on and on, but I mention these four companies because they were not convicted only once, as were the labour people of whom I spoke a few moments ago, but twice of breaking the law.
Let us look at how serious a view the court took of their offences. For example, in 1958 Bathurst Power and Paper Company was fined the tremendous amount of $7,000 for breaking the law, although in that year it made a net profit after taxes of $1,500,000. The Gair Company was fined $3,000. I cannot find a figure for its net profit because it is a wholly owned subsidiary of a United States company and does not issue a financial statement. In 1958 Hinde and Dauche was fined $3,000, having made a net profit of $1,323,000. For violating the anti-combines law the St. Lawrence Corporation was fined $3,000, having made a profit in 1958 of $5,740,000. If there ever was a cheap licence for stealing, the anti-combines law provides it.
Let us look at the directors of these corporations, as shown in the records published by the Financial Post. They are some of the most influential and respected people in Canada. On the board of directors of the Bathurst Power and Paper Company, when it was convicted of violating the anticombines legislation, was a name that hon. members of this house well know: R. H. Winters. On the board of St. Lawrence Corporation in 1959, when it was convicted, were the names of M. W. McCutcheon and E. P. Taylor. E. P. Taylor was chairman of the board of the St. Lawrence Corporation when the company was convicted in 1965. On the board of directors of Hinde and Dauche in 1959 appeared

Mr. Speaker, it is time we focused our attention more sharply in this country on our anti-combines legislation. I think there is much concern about the practices of the past. I think the government is indicating that it wishes to concentrate its efforts more and more on this aspect of public policy.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
When the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) announced the government's plans to reorganize ministerial responsibility for several government departments last December, he said that the responsibility for special areas of legislation concerning the national interest in the conduct of business activity, which had previously been shared by the Department of Justice and the Department of the Secretary of State, would be placed under the control of a new and separate minister. These included the Bankruptcy Act, the Companies Act, combines investigation and research, patents and copyrights, trade marks and similar matters. He said that the responsibility for some of these functions would be transferred to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Favreau). Under the Public Service Rearrangement and Transfer of Duties Act, the powers, duties and functions of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Cardin) under the Combines Investigation Act, other than those vested in him as Attorney General of Canada, and certain others, were transferred to the President of the Privy Council effective January 1, 1966.
Then, Mr. Speaker, on May 9, 1966, first reading was given to a bill respecting the organization of the government of Canada, which was subsequently enacted and given royal assent on June 16, 1966. This statute, among other things, establishes a new department called the Department of the Registrar General, and the Registrar General's duties are described as including all matters over which the parliament of Canada has jurisdiction, not by law assigned to any other department, branch or agency of the Canadian
November 4, 1966	COMMONS
government, relating to (a) combines, mergers, monopolies in restraint of trade; (b) patents and trade marks; (c) bankruptcy and insolvency and (d) corporate affairs.
This act was to come into force when promulgated, and I believe it has now been promulgated so that we have a new department concentrating on these business problems which involve the government of Canada. As a result I hope that the problems of combines, mergers and monopolies in restraint of trade are going to receive greater attention than they have ever had given to them previously.
We are fortunate in this country in having a very able director of investigation and research under the Combines Investigation Act. He and his staff have been most active, and I am sure that what this house would like to do is to see that they are given every tool necessary with which to protect the public interest.
The hon. member who introduced Bill No. C-30 has suggested that certain minimum penalties be imposed. I think there is no question that under the combines legislation the penalties imposed have been completely inadequate. They have been treated very much as mere licence fees and I think the provisions for deterring offences in this field must be re-examined and more effective deterrents found. However, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that the proposal in Bill No. C-30 is inconsistent with the whole trend of current philosophy relating to minimum penalties in criminal law. As I understand it, the trend is away from minimum penalties. Minimum penalties tend to restrict a court in the exercise of its discretion and, generally speaking, in criminal law this discretion should be preserved as far as possible.
There are certain practical reasons why the discretion of the court should be preserved in this particular field of criminal law. For instance, the persons who are officers or directors of companies being prosecuted under the legislation are frequently required as witnesses, and of course they could not be required to testify against themselves. I am sure others are found to be aged or infirm and on humanitarian grounds would not normally be prosecuted.
Surely the net which Bill C-30 attempts to cast to make all directors liable is too broad. For instance, certain conscientious officers might actively seek to prevent breaches of the combines act by their company's policy

Another factor is that there is a great turnover of officers and directors in companies, and the suggestion that on a second or third offence there must be a mandatory jail term imposed raises the possibility that persons sentenced in such a way would be ones different from the officers or directors who were involved in the first offence.
Another very practical objection to specifying a minimum penalty here or in any other criminal or quasi-criminal legislation is that the minimum may tend to become the norm. This is very clearly illustrated by the experience since the ceiling on fines was lifted from this act in 1952. Before that there were numerous complaints from judges that the ceiling on fines was low, and I would like to refer to some comments to this effect.
Mr. Justice Schroeder in Regina v. Firestone Tire and Rubber Company of Canada Limited et al, reported in "1954 Ontario Weekly Notes" at page 68, is reported as saying at page 73:
In my view, the maximum penalty of $10,000 provided by the Code is wholly inadequate to meet the ends of justice even as a punishment to the least of these offenders.
Mr. Justice Judson in Regina v. Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation Ltd. et al, reported in "1956 Ontario Weekly Notes" at page 753, is reported on page 754 as follows:
What does direct my judgment on the question of the amount of the fine is this: the duration of the conspiracy, almost 20 years; the complete control of the industry through the agreement in the matter of price and the condition of sale.
Even a modest participant in a conspiracy of that kind, lasting as long as this one lasted, is a person who should be told, and told in no uncertain terms, that this conduct is prohibited and, in my opinion, obviously prohibited by the Criminal Code, that any participant must have realized what he was doing and that to talk about a modest fine in those circumstances is quite out of the question. The expression has been used by some of the judges that even the maximum fine under this statute, as it stood before amendment, was no more than a licence fee. and a very moderate licence fee.
It is quite impossible to regard a conspiracy of this kind as a minor commercial misdemeanour. It is a serious offence against the Criminal Code and I think it calls for the maximum fine, in the case of all the participants, and each company will be fined $10,000.

Various other comments in a similar vein were made by judges prior to 1952, but the interesting thing is that since the ceiling on fines was lilted there has been no increase in the quantum of any fine beyond the previous maximum.
Rather than the solution proposed by Bill C-30, it is my submission that what really is required is that the courts be encouraged to be much more realistic in sentencing. The Exchequer Court of Canada was given jurisdiction to try combines offences in 1960 and some proceedings already have been taken in that court. I believe, however, that an attempt should be made to develop the experience of that court so that we may have a corps of judges familiar with the anti-combines legislation who will be much better equipped than the regular criminal courts to deal with the problem of sentencing on a uniform, realistic and effective basis.
Beyond the question of criminal liability I believe there is a field which has been sadly neglected, and that is the field of civil liability on the part of companies which have offended against our anti-combines legislation. In Bill C-30 I notice that section 7 provides that section 35 of the act be repealed and a section substituted which provides an additional money penalty where the crime has caused anyone financial injury. But in reading the proposed new section 35 one sees that subsection (2) begins:
Where an injured party is awarded damages against any person in a civil action as remedy for a wrong done-
The difficulty which is apparent here is that it has been held by the Supreme Court of Canada that the Combines Investigation Act creates no civil right of action. In the Supreme Court of Canada, in the case of Direct Lumber Company Limited v. Western Plywood Company Limited, Mr. Justice Judson, in a decision given on behalf of the court on June 25, 1962, said in part:
In any event, in my respectful opinion, the judgment under appeal is correct and neither section-
He is speaking here of sections of the Criminal Code.
-gives a cause of action in damages to a person who alleges a breach of these sections by a defendant.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I think the government of Canada could be much more venturesome in attempting to provide some real deterrent in respect of a breach of the law in this field

and in providing some protection for consumers. This is something which I do not think Bill C-30 accomplishes at all. I believe our principal concern should be the protection of the consumers. Under its powers in the field of trade and commerce this parliament should be able to enact legislation which would make it possible to impose a civil liability on offending companies under the Combines Investigation Act.
I think Bill C-30 tends to be impractical in the accomplishment of the aims which it seems to have. Its minimum penalty provisions are not consistent with the trend of thinking in the whole field of criminal law. I believe the remedy, in the field of a deterrent, lies in better trained judges and perhaps prosecutors. I feel this is an area of law which has been neglected and should be examined most carefully by the new Department of the Registrar General with a view to obtaining some recompense for consumers who have suffered damages as a result of offences under this act.
