Mr. Speaker, I think the matter now under discussion is a very worth-while one indeed. Over the past couple of years we have noted an attempt by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) to bring this matter to the attention of the house. I believe this bill, or one very similar to it, has been on the order paper for some time. When the hon. member began his remarks I noticed that he enunciated the very laudable principle that the law must treat all people equally. Notwithstanding the progress which has been made in many areas and in many fields over the past century, or just about a century, in this country in an attempt to attain this laudable principle, we still find situations where there certainly is prima facie evidence, I suggest, that the law is not doing all it ought to do to protect the rights of some and to curtail the activities of others.
It seems to me that while all of us pay lip service to this laudable goal and while we all bear in mind the sort of constant and continual battle that we have had in attempting to make this principle as true as possible, one of the paramount ingredients for success for anyone, for any group, for any party or for any government striving to achieve this goal is that one must take on approach to the problem which is as broad as possible. There
November 4, 1966

are the usual technical criticisms of this bill which anybody could make of any bill, some of which are quite worthy and some rather picayune. The hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Stanbury) may have a lot more people in his area than there are in Prince Edward Island, and there are those who believe that quantity is a substitute for quality, but I am one who believes that quantity is not a substitute for quality.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
In his remarks he referred to some of the technical weaknesses of the bill, and if time permits perhaps I too may find myself dealing with some of these technical weaknesses. However, at the outset I think the fundamental weakness of the approach of the hon. member is one of principle. He has adopted what I would call, not unkindly, a reactionary approach to the problem, that is to say, he is treating this whole matter solely within the confines of criminal law.
I think it is fair to say, as I believe my colleague implied, that the federal government under successive administrations to date has been rather timid in broadening the approach to this problem. Perhaps my hon. friend from Winnipeg North suffers from the same inhibitions as many of those who have sat on this side for a long period of time.
I feel we could deal with this problem more effectively if we recognized that under the trade and commerce clause of our constitution possibilities are open to the government to expand what I would call the economic approach under combines legislation. Not only would it serve, in my view, a useful purpose in protecting the rights of individuals by seeing to it that other individuals, those infringing the law or behaving badly, acted according to a national consensus but it would at the same time assist in a positive manner, not only prohibit in a negative way, the development of our country.
In regard to combines there may in fact be situations where it might be to the economic well-being of the country and the interest of the individual, in attempting to achieve competitive efficiency with industry abroad, to use this sort of economic device. I would have thought that the hon. member for Winnipeg North, bearing the New Democratic Party label, might have thought of this approach himself, but perhaps even the New Democratic Party has its left and right wings.

We as the sort of collective wisdom of Canada find this from time to time of interest and challenge, particularly when we are watching this phenomenon in action.
There is reference in the bill or in the remarks of the hon. member to the use of injunctions. We now have such use on the criminal side and it seems to me that we could be using injunctions as economic weapons as well which would, of course, open the door to civil remedies. The hon. gentleman tried to use an interesting device when he talked of forfeiture. That is an interesting and novel device, and perhaps to the complete reactionary it might even be something of an innovation, particularly considering the use of forfeiture as a way of providing damages to an individual.
If we look at the broader approach of combines legislation, not only in the limited sense of performing the task, which we all agree it has not performed sufficiently to date, but of protecting the people and curtailing certain individuals, this may be a useful device. It might be useful in respect of such things as economic planning. This may not really be a part of my hon. friend's philosophy, but we could use the combines legislation to provide some of the really forceful and meaningful improvements that could be brought about by this government which has in its short term of office, barely three and a half years, dealt with many of the problems of making people equal under the law and seeing to it that the law treats all people equally. Notwithstanding the progress of the past three years, it seems to me this is one area in the continuing battle where the federal government to date has not displayed that ingredient of daring that we expect. No doubt, bearing in mind the recent changes in the structure of the ministry, we can look forward in the not too distant future to this kind of an approach.
It is with the confidence that this will be done that I make the remainder of my remarks. I do hope the government will attack this problem on a broader economic front and use the powers under the trade and commerce clause of our constitution which, as I said, could be a useful tool in protecting the individual and attaining the goals which the hon. member seeks to achieve in his limited approach contained in Bill C-30.

Under the broader approach I am advocating civil remedies could be used and damages secured. This is a practice followed in the United States and I believe in the United Kingdom. In those countries as high as triple damages are awarded, and I certainly would not object to the government attempting to obtain triple damages under this new approach. My colleague, the hon. member for York-Scarborough, has made reference to the effect that this will have for the consumer, and I think it is a major effect.
Let me again refer to the long-term effect that the proper use of combines legislation could have on our economic development. It seems to me that if we use it as a proper tool in economic planning and development we could allow when it is in the interests of Canada, having regard to the individual, certain interests to behave in a manner which would give them some advantage in international competition. This is perhaps the direction in which this country ought to be heading in the next decade. We have heard a great deal of talk about the direction of our economy. On the one hand we have those who follow the school of thought concerned about ownership in this country while on the other we have those who advocate the con-tinentalist approach. As one might expect, I do not necessarily subscribe to either school of thought and certainly I do not think this is the time for me to deal with either at any length.
It seems to me that a middle course of action would be consistent with the development of Canada, one which would give us a new kind of role in our international attempt to create an efficient economy which could compete on a world-wide basis. I think this can be done on an industry by industry basis and perhaps would move us in a sense toward international free trade as opposed to free trade with one country.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
I believe that ultimately we can create a unique Canadian economy, and one statute that can play an important role in what I believe to be the most acceptable approach to Canadian development is the combines legislation. I think it is important that this matter has been discussed in the house. I recognize the fact that the bill has been on the order paper for three years, and I congratulate the hon. member for his interest in this field. It is undoubtedly an area in which we have not done all the things we should have done.

The one thought I should like to leave with you, Mr. Speaker, is that while we have many problems and many areas that we could tackle in ensuring that all men are treated equally, when we do tackle these areas let us do so in as progressive and enlightened a manner as possible. I think that the approach of the hon. member in confining his bill to the criminal aspect of this problem is too limited for Canada in the 1960's.

I wish to refer to the service the hon. gentleman has rendered the house in placing on Hansard the information to which he alluded earlier in the debate in regard to the fines imposed under the Combines Investigation Act for combining against the consumer. On June 27, 1966, as reported at page 6857 of Hansard, the hon. member for Winnipeg North asked the following question:
In the past ten years, in how many cases did the government charge and prosecute companies for violations of the Combines Act, except for cases under section 33(c)?
Then he asked for the names of the companies involved in each case, and the fines imposed by the courts. The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Favreau) made the return to this question. There follows in Hansard a very long table of names of companies and the fines imposed upon them for combining and conspiring to rig prices against the consumer.
It is interesting to look at this table, not in the way my hon. friend did by picking out a couple of directors, one of whom happens to be a member of parliament and the other a senator, not with a view to trying to attach blame to any particular individual but to see what has happened in Canada in this respect. For instance, with regard to wire fencing we see that six companies were prosecuted and the fine levied was $10,000 in each instance. As was said earlier in the debate when hon. members referred to cases which had come before the courts, judges consider this penalty to be simply a licence for going ahead with rigging prices against the consumer. 1 ask my western friends on the other side of the house what we think of eastern manufacturers who combine to rig the price of the fencing we place around our farms and ship it to us in
